Section : Geography Basics

- Geography as a discipline - Introduction to geography as a subject - Prior study and transition - You have studied geography within Social Science up to the secondary stage, gaining awareness of geographical phenomena across the world and its regions - Now, as an independent subject, geography explores the earth’s physical environment, human activities, and their interrelationships - Purpose of studying geography - A key question arises: Why study geography? - We live on the earth’s surface, and our lives are shaped by our surroundings in numerous ways - We rely on resources from our environment for survival - Primitive societies depended on natural means of subsistence like edible plants and animals - Over time, humans developed technologies to produce food using resources such as land, soil, and water, adapting food habits and clothing to weather conditions - Defining geography - Core concept - What is geography? - Earth is our home, shared with many creatures, big and small, who live and sustain themselves on it - The term "geography" was coined by Eratosthenes (father of geography), a Greek scholar (276-194 BC), from Greek roots "geo" (earth) and "graphos" (description), meaning "description of the earth" - Scholars define it as "the description of the earth as the abode [place of residence] of human beings" - Focus of study - Geography studies variations across the earth’s surface: - Physical features include mountains, hills, valleys, plains, plateaus, oceans, lakes, deserts, and wilderness - Social and cultural features include villages, cities, roads, railways, ports, markets, and other human creations developed over time - These variations reveal the relationship between the physical environment and social/cultural features - The physical environment sets the stage for human societies to display their creative skills using tools and techniques developed through cultural evolution - - Scope and approach of geography - Interdisciplinary nature - Geography integrates data from natural sciences (e.g., geology, pedology, oceanography, botany, zoology, meteorology) and social sciences (e.g., economics, history, sociology, political science, anthropology) - It differs from other sciences in its subject matter and methodology but is closely related to them, synthesizing their insights - Analytical focus - Geography examines: - Variations in phenomena over space (areal differentiation) - Associations between phenomena and factors causing these variations (e.g., cropping patterns varying due to soils, climates, market demands, farmer investment, and technology) - Causal relationships between phenomena, aiding interpretation and prediction - Geographical phenomena, both physical and human, are dynamic, changing over time due to interactions between the evolving earth and active humans - Nature and human interactions - Integrated relationship - Geography studies the interplay between nature and humans as an integrated whole - Humans are part of nature, leaving imprints on it, while nature influences human life (e.g., food, clothing, shelter, occupation) - Historical and modern dynamics - Primitive societies directly depended on their immediate environment - Modern societies use technology to modify the environment, expanding their scope by utilizing natural resources - Impact of technology - Technology has: - Reduced the harshness of labor and increased efficiency - Provided leisure for higher pursuits - Boosted production scale and labor mobility - Poetic representation - A poetic dialogue captures this interaction: - Nature (God): "You created the soil, I created the cup; you created night, I created the lamp; you created wilderness, hilly terrains, and deserts; I created flower beds and gardens" - Humans have moved from necessity to freedom, humanizing nature while nature naturalizes humans - Spatial [relating to or occupying space] organization and integration - Spatial framework - Geography organizes space through transportation and communication networks, linking routes and settlements (nodes) of varying types and hierarchies - As a social science, geography focuses on spatial [relating to or occupying space] organization and integration - Key questions - It addresses three key questions: - What? - Identifying patterns of natural and cultural features on the earth’s surface - Where? - Examining the distribution of these features - Why? - Explaining causal relationships, processes, and phenomena behind these patterns - The "what" and "where" questions provide inventory data, popular during colonial times, but the "why" question elevates geography to a scientific discipline - Skills and tools in geography - Capabilities developed - Geography equips you to: - Appreciate diversity and investigate causes of spatial and temporal [secular / non-spiritual] variations - Convert the globe into maps, developing a visual sense of the earth’s surface - Use modern techniques like GIS and computer cartography to contribute to national development - Geography as an integrating discipline - Holistic nature of geography - Spatial and temporal synthesis [the combination of components or elements to form a connected whole] - Geography synthesizes spatially, while history synthesizes temporally, recognizing [identifying] the world as a system of interdependencies - Today’s world is a "global village" due to improved transportation, accessibility, and technology (e.g., audio-visual media, IT) - Technology enhances monitoring of natural, economic, and social phenomena - Interdisciplinary connections - Integration with sciences - Geography interfaces with numerous natural and social sciences, all aiming to understand reality - It comprehends phenomena associations holistically [individual parts can't be considered, instead whole system is considered] in a spatial context [circumstances], differing across places - Historical examples - Examples of integration: - Spatial distance and depth (e.g., oceans, large land areas) have historically influenced events, providing defense or altering outcomes - In India, the Himalayas acted as barriers and routes for migrants/invaders, while the sea coast facilitated (make easy) contacts with East/Southeast Asia, Europe, and Africa - European navigation technology enabled colonization of Asia and Africa, including India - Time as a dimension - Temporal dynamics - Geographical phenomena change over time (e.g., landforms, climate, vegetation, economic activities, cultural developments) - Time and space are interchangeable (e.g., 1,500 km = 2 hours by plane or 17 hours by train) - Time is the fourth dimension in geography, alongside three spatial dimensions (please specify the other three: length, width, height) - Physical geography and natural sciences - Connections and tools - Branches like geomorphology, climatology, oceanography, and soil geography link to geology, meteorology, hydrology, and pedology, deriving [obtain / acquire] data from them - Biogeography connects to botany, zoology, and ecology, studying human niches - Tools: - Maps require proficiency [skillful] in mathematics (projections, statistics, econometrics) and art (drawing, sketches) - Geography uses astronomical locations (latitudes, longitudes) and converts the geoid earth into two-dimensional maps - Geography and social sciences - Links to social disciplines - History links to geography through spatial influences on events - Geographical thought, as a philosophical root, traces the discipline’s evolution - Social sciences (sociology, political science, economics, demography) study social reality with spatial aspects, aligning with branches like social, political, economic, and population geography - Political geography examines territory, people, sovereignty, and political behavior - Economic geography studies spatial aspects of production, distribution, exchange, and consumption - Population geography aligns with demography (growth, distribution, migration, etc.) - Branches of geography - Approaches to study - Study methods - Geography is interdisciplinary [relating to more than one branch of knowledge], studied via: - Systematic approach (by Alexander von Humboldt, 1769-1859): Examines phenomena globally, identifying typologies (e.g., studying vegetation worldwide, then classifying equatorial or monsoon forests) - - Regional approach (by Karl Ritter, 1779-1859): Divides the world into regions (natural, political, designated) for holistic study - - Dualism exists: Early focus was on physical geography, but human geography emerged due to humans’ integral role in nature - Branches based on systematic approach - Physical geography - Sub-branches - Geomorphology: Studies landforms, their evolution, and processes - Climatology: Examines atmosphere structure, weather, climates, and types - Hydrology: Investigates water (oceans, lakes, rivers) and its effects on life - Soil geography: Analyzes soil formation, types, fertility, distribution, and use - Importance - Covers lithosphere (landforms, relief), atmosphere (weather, climate), hydrosphere (oceans, lakes), and biosphere (life forms, food chains, ecological balance) - Landforms support agriculture (plains), resources (plateaus), and water (mountains) - Climate affects housing, clothing, farming, and industries; humans modify it with technology (e.g., air conditioners) - Precipitation drives agriculture and groundwater recharge - Oceans provide fish, minerals (e.g., manganese nodules [small rounded lumps] in India) - Soils, renewable yet influenced by nature and culture, support agriculture and the biosphere - Additional insight - Geography describes and explains areal differentiation (Richard Hartshorne, Hettner) - It manages natural resources, balancing human use and ecological sustainability - Human geography - Sub-branches - Social/cultural geography: Studies society, spatial dynamics, and cultural contributions - Population and settlement geography: Analyzes population (growth, density, migration) and settlements (rural, urban) - Economic geography: Examines economic activities (agriculture, industry, trade, transport) - Historical geography: Studies historical processes shaping spatial organization - Political geography: Focuses on political events, boundaries, constituencies, and behavior - Biogeography - Sub-branches - Plant geography: Studies vegetation patterns in habitats - Zoo geography: Examines animal distributions and habitats - Ecology/ecosystem: Analyzes species habitats scientifically - Environmental geography: Addresses land degradation, pollution, and conservation - Branches based on regional approach - Regional branches - 1. Regional studies/area studies: Includes macro, meso, and micro levels - 2. Regional planning: Covers rural/country and urban/town planning - 3. Regional development - 4. Regional analysis - Common aspects across disciplines - Philosophy and methods - Philosophy: - Geographical thought - Land and human interaction/human ecology - Methods and techniques: - Cartography, including computer cartography (science of drawing maps) - Quantitative/statistical techniques - Field survey methods - Geo-informatics (remote sensing, GIS, GPS) - Geography evolves with technology (e.g., manual to computer cartography, GIS, GPS), enhancing data handling and analysis (see *Practical Work in Geography – Part I*, NCERT, 2006) - The origin and evolution of the universe - Introduction to the chapter - Motivation and purpose - Starry nights have always attracted us since childhood - You may also have thought of these stars and had numerous questions in your mind - Questions such as how many stars are there in the sky? How did they come into existence? Can one reach the end of the sky? - May be many more such questions are still there in your mind - In this chapter, you will learn how these “twinkling little stars” were formed - With that you will eventually also read the story of origin and evolution of the earth - Light year - A light year is a measure of distance and not of time - Light travels at a speed of 300,000 km/second - Considering this, the distances the light will travel in one year is taken to be one light year - This equals to 9.461×10 12 km - The mean distance between the sun and the earth is 149,598,000 km - In terms of light years, it is 8.311minutes - Universe and it's origin - The universe is vast expanse of space that contains all matter and energy in existence. It's exact size is still unknown and recent researches showing it's expansion. - Early views before on universe - Geocentric view (Geocentrism) - According to this view, earth is at the centre of the universe and other bodies revolve around it. - Most religions believed in this view. - Heliocentric view (Heliocentrism) - In this view, sun is at the centre and all bodies including earth revolved around it. - Aristarchus, a Greek philosopher was the first to put forward helio centric view. - Modern theories on the origin of the universe - Big Bang theory (expanding universe hypothesis) - - Overview - The most popular argument regarding the origin of the universe is the Big Bang Theory - It is also called expanding universe hypothesis - Edwin Hubble, in 1920, provided evidence that the universe is expanding - As time passes, galaxies move further and further apart - Balloon analogy - You can experiment and find what does the expanding universe mean - Take a balloon and mark some points on it to represent the galaxies - Now, if you start inflating the balloon, the points marked on the balloon will appear to be moving away from each other as the balloon expands - Similarly, the distance between the galaxies is also found to be increasing and thereby, the universe is considered to be expanding - However, you will find that besides the increase in the distances between the points on the balloon, the points themselves are expanding - This is not in accordance with the fact - Scientists believe that though the space between the galaxies is increasing, observations do not support the expansion of galaxies - So, the balloon example is only partially correct - Stages of development in accordance with big bang - In the beginning, all matter forming the universe existed in one place in the form of a “tiny ball” (singular atom) with an unimaginably small volume, infinite temperature and infinite density - At the Big Bang the “tiny ball” exploded violently - This led to a huge expansion - It is now generally accepted that the event of big bang took place 13.7 billion years before the present - The expansion continues even to the present day - As it grew, some energy was converted into matter - There was particularly rapid expansion within fractions of a second after the bang - Thereafter, the expansion has slowed down - Within first three minutes from the Big Bang event, the first atom began to form - Within 300,000 years from the Big Bang, temperature dropped to 4,500 K (Kelvin) and gave rise to atomic matter - The universe became transparent - Steady state theory (Hoyle's concept of steady state) - - The expansion of universe means increase in space between the galaxies - An alternative to this was Hoyle’s concept of steady (stable / balance) state - It considered the universe to be roughly the same at any point of time - However, with greater evidence becoming available about the expanding universe, scientific community at present favours argument of expanding universe - Celestial bodies - Galaxies - A galaxy is a huge collection of gas, dust, and billions of stars and their solar systems. - A galaxy contains a large number of stars - Galaxies spread over vast distances that are measured in thousands of light-years - The diameters of individual galaxies range from 80,000-150,000 light years - Types of galaxies - - Spiral galaxies - Spiral galaxies have active star formation in their arms and in their nuclei. - Elliptical galaxies - Elliptical galaxies generally contain older stars and have less active star formation compared to spiral galaxies. - Irregular galaxies - Some irregular galaxies exhibit high rates of star formation, while others are more quiescent [inactive / inert]. - Milky way - - It is a spiral galaxy in which our solar system is located. - It's about 100,000 light years across or about 30 kpc - The Sun does not lie near the center of our Galaxy. It lies about 8 kpc from the center on what is known as the Orion Arm of the Milky Way. - It contains super massive black hole "Sagittarius A*" at it's centre. - Andromeda galaxy is the closest neighboring galaxy to milky way. It is also a spiral galaxy and expected to collide with milky way in far future. - In ancient India, our galaxy was imagined to be a river of light flowing in the sky. Thus, it was named Akash Ganga. - The galaxy formation - Initial conditions - The distribution of matter and energy was not even in the early universe - These initial density differences gave rise to differences in gravitational forces and it caused the matter to get drawn together - These formed the bases for development of galaxies - Formation process - A galaxy starts to form by accumulation of hydrogen gas in the form of a very large cloud called nebula - Eventually, growing nebula develops localised clumps of gas - These clumps continue to grow into even denser gaseous bodies, giving rise to formation of stars - The formation of stars is believed to have taken place some 5-6 billion years ago - Stars - A star is a massive, luminous sphere of plasma held together by its own gravity, generating light and heat through nuclear fusion. - Star formation - - Star life cycle - - Sun is also a star. - It is estimated to be 5 billion years old and has a diameter of 1.4 million kilometers. - It is approximately 150 million km away from the earth. - Temperature varies from layers. - - The solar corona is hotter than the photosphere because of non-thermal heating mechanisms, specifically magnetic fields and waves. - These mechanisms transport energy from the Sun's interior to the upper atmosphere, where it's released as heat, creating the corona's high temperatures. - In essence, the corona is hotter than the photosphere because the energy that fuels the Sun is being transported and dissipated in the outer atmosphere, rather than being released at the surface. - The Sun's mass is approximately 333,000 times greater than Earth's mass. It accounts for 99.83% of the mass of the solar system. - Its diameter is about 109 times that of Earth's. - It is 150.92 million km away from earth and this distance is also called 1 astronomical unit. - The sun is powered by nuclear fusion, where hydrogen atoms fuse into helium, releasing tremendous energy in the process. - This energy is then radiated outward, ultimately reaching Earth as light and heat. Additionally, the sun's magnetic field plays a role in phenomena like solar flares and the solar wind. - Sun spots - Sunspots are dark spots on the Sun's surface that appear darker than the surrounding areas due to being cooler, but still very hot. - They are caused by strong magnetic fields that inhibit convection, preventing heat from reaching the surface. Sunspots are also visible manifestations of the Sun's active regions, which are sources of solar eruptions. - Sunspots are located on the outermost layer of the Sun called 'Photosphere'. - Solar winds - Solar wind is a stream of charged particles (mainly protons and electrons) emitted from the Sun's corona. - The interaction of the solar wind with Earth's upper atmosphere can create the beautiful aurora borealis (northern lights) and aurora australis (southern lights). - Solar wind variations, particularly during solar storms, can impact satellites, communication networks, and even power grids by releasing bursts of charged particles that interact with Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field. - Pole star (North star) - The Pole Star, also known as Polaris, is a prominent star in the night sky located nearly directly above Earth's North Pole. - It is part of the constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Bear) and is famous for being used as a navigational aid because it remains almost stationary in the sky, with all other stars appearing to rotate around it. - Constellations - - - Constellations are groupings of stars that form patterns or shapes in the sky. These patterns are typically named after mythological figures, animals, or objects. - Types of Constellations: - Zodiac Constellations: - These constellations lie along the ecliptic, the apparent path that the Sun traces through the sky. There are 12 traditional zodiac signs, each associated with a constellation. The Sun, Moon, and planets appear to pass through these constellations in the course of the year. - The 12 zodiac constellations are: - Aries (The Ram) - Taurus (The Bull) - Gemini (The Twins) - Cancer (The Crab) - Leo (The Lion) - Virgo (The Virgin) - Libra (The Scales) - Scorpius (The Scorpion) - Sagittarius (The Archer) - Capricornus (The Goat) - Aquarius (The Water Bearer) - Pisces (The Fishes) - Non-Zodiac Constellations: - These constellations do not lie along the ecliptic and are spread across the sky. - Some famous non-zodiac constellations include: - Orion (The Hunter) - Ursa Major (The Great Bear) - Ursa Minor (The Little Bear) - Cassiopeia (The Queen) - Cygnus (The Swan) - Lyra (The Lyre) - Andromeda (The Princess) - Leo (The Lion) - Scorpius (The Scorpion) - Importance of Constellations: - Navigation: - Historically, constellations have been used for navigation, particularly by sailors and explorers, to help them find their way across vast oceans and unfamiliar lands. - Astronomical Observation: - Constellations serve as a reference point for locating celestial objects like stars, planets, and galaxies in the night sky. - Cultural Significance: - Many cultures around the world have different myths and stories associated with constellations, and these stories have been passed down through generations. - Planets - The word ‘planet’ comes from the Greek word “Planetai” which means ‘wanderers’. - A planet is a celestial body that orbits a star (like the Sun), is large enough for its own gravity to make it spherical, and has cleared its orbital path of other objects - Pluto was re-categorized as dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbital path of other objects - Stages of development - - The stars are localised lumps of gas within a nebula - The gravitational force within the lumps leads to the formation of a core to the gas cloud and a huge rotating disc of gas and dust develops around the gas core - In the next stage, the gas cloud starts getting condensed and the matter around the core develops into small-rounded objects - These small-rounded objects by the process of cohesion [togetherness] develop into what is called planetesimals (minute planet) - Larger bodies start forming by collision, and gravitational attraction causes the material to stick together - Planetesimals are a large number of smaller bodies - In the final stage, these large number of small planetesimals accrete [grow by accumulation] to form a fewer large bodies in the form of planets - Orbit - All planets revolve around a star (like the Sun) in fixed paths called orbits, which are generally elliptical (elongated) in shape. - Earth is also a planet - Early theories on the origin of the earth - Overview - A large number of hypotheses [theory / speculation / supposition] were put forth by different philosophers and scientists regarding the origin of the earth - Nebular hypothesis - One of the earlier and popular arguments was by German philosopher Immanuel Kant - Mathematician Laplace revised it in 1796 - It is known as Nebular Hypothesis - The hypothesis considered that the planets were formed out of a cloud of material associated with a youthful sun, which was slowly rotating - Chamberlain and Moulton hypothesis - Later in 1900, Chamberlain and Moulton considered that a wandering star approached the sun - As a result, a cigar-shaped extension of material was separated from the solar surface - As the passing star moved away, the material separated from the solar surface continued to revolve around the sun and it slowly condensed into planets - Sir James Jeans and later Sir Harold Jeffrey supported this argument - Binary theories - At a later date, the arguments considered of a companion to the sun to have been coexisting - These arguments are called binary theories - Revised nebular hypothesis - In 1950, Otto Schmidt in Russia and Carl Weizascar in Germany somewhat revised the ‘nebular hypothesis’, though differing in details - They considered that the sun was surrounded by solar nebula containing mostly the hydrogen and helium along with what may be termed as dust - The friction and collision of particles led to formation of a disk-shaped cloud and the planets were formed through the process of accretion [accumulation / gathering / amassing] - Shift in focus - However, scientists in later period took up the problems of origin of universe rather than that of just the earth or the planets - The formation of moon (once part of earth) - The moon is the only natural satellite of the earth, its diametre is only one-quarter that of the earth. - A satellite is any object that orbits around a larger body in space due to gravitational attraction. - Types of satellites: - Natural Satellites: - These are celestial bodies like moons that orbit planets. - Example: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. - Artificial Satellites: - Man-made objects launched into orbit for various purposes. - Used for communication, weather forecasting, navigation, Earth observation, and scientific research. - Example: INSAT, GPS, Hubble Space Telescope. - It is about 3,84,400 km away from the earth. - It has mountains plains and depressions on its surface. These cast shadows on the moon’s surface. - Neil Armstrong was the first man to step on the surface of the moon on 21 July 1969. - The moon moves around the earth in about 27 days. - It takes exactly the same time to complete one spin. - As a result, only one side of the moon is visible to us on the earth. - Theories of formation - Early theory - Like the origin of the earth, there have been attempts to explain how the moon was formed - In 1838, Sir George Darwin suggested that initially, the earth and the moon formed a single rapidly rotating body - The whole mass became a dumb-bell-shaped body and eventually it broke - It was also suggested that the material forming the moon was separated from what we have at present the depression occupied by the Pacific Ocean - Current theory - - However, the present scientists do not accept either of the explanations - It is now generally believed that the formation of moon, as a satellite of the earth, is an outcome of ‘giant impact’ or what is described as “the big splat” - A body of the size of one to three times that of mars collided into the earth sometime shortly after the earth was formed - It blasted a large part of the earth into space - This portion of blasted material then continued to orbit the earth and eventually formed into the present moon about 4.44 billion years ago - Dwarf planets - Dwarf planets are celestial bodies that orbit the Sun, are massive enough to be nearly round due to their gravity, but have not cleared their orbital path of other objects. - Asteroid and comets - Asteroid - Asteroids are small, rocky objects that orbit the sun, often found in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. They are remnants of the solar system's formation and can range in size from boulders to objects hundreds of miles in diameter. - Asteroids are generally made of rock, dust, and frozen ices. - The vast majority of asteroids in solar system reside in the main asteroid belt, located between Mars and Jupiter. - Example: Ceres (largest asteroid), Vesta, Eros, Bennu - Comets - Comets are icy, small solar system bodies that orbit the Sun. They are composed of frozen gases, dust, and rocks and are often described as "dirty snowballs". - Comets in solar system are believed to originate from two primary regions: the Kuiper Belt and the Oort Cloud. - Asteroids are primarily made of rock and metal, while comets are composed of ice, dust, and rocky material - Examples : Halley's Comet, Hale-Bopp, and Hyakutake. - Meteors, meteoroids and meteorites - Meteoroids are small pieces of rock or metal orbiting the star. When a meteoroid enters a planet's atmosphere, it becomes a meteor, creating a streak of light as it burns up. If a meteoroid survives the atmospheric entry, it becomes a meteorite and lands on the planet. - The term is not only specific to Earth, but is valid for any planet. - The primary difference between a meteoroid and an asteroid lies in their size. - Asteroids are generally larger than meteoroids, with a minimum size of 1 meter (3.28 feet) in diameter. Meteoroids, on the other hand, are smaller, ranging from dust particles to objects up to 1 meter across. - Our solar system - - Overview - Composition - Our solar system consists of the sun (the star), 8 planets, 63 moons, millions of smaller bodies like asteroids and comets and huge quantity of dust-grains and gases - Formation timeline - The nebula from which our Solar system is supposed to have been formed, started its collapse and core formation some time 5-5.6 billion years ago and the planets were formed about 4.6 billion years ago - All the planets were formed in the same period sometime about 4.6 billion years ago - Planet classification in solar system - - Inner planets (Terrestrial planets / Earth like planets) - Out of the eight planets - Mercury - It is the smallest, nearest (to sun), and fastest - Venus (also referred as Earth's twin or sister) - Most planets rotate in counterclockwise direction, the same direction they orbit the sun. - But it rotates in clockwise direction as an exception, one theory for this unusual rotation is that it was knocked off its upright position earlier in its history - The other exception is Uranus which spins in clockwise direction. - It is also the hottest planet - Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being further from sun primarily due to its dense, carbon dioxide-rich atmosphere, which creates a strong greenhouse effect. - Earth - The earth is the third nearest planet to the sun. - In size, it is the fifth largest planet. - It is slightly flattened at the poles. That is why, its shape is described as a - Geoid. Geoid means an earth-like shape. - The earth is neither too hot nor too cold. It has water and air, which are very essential for our survival. - Mars (also called red planet due to iron presence) - These are called as the inner planets as they lie between the sun and the belt of asteroids - Alternatively, the first four are called Terrestrial, meaning earth-like as they are made up of rock and metals, and have relatively high densities - Outer planets (Jovian planets / Jupiter like planets / gas giants) - The other four planets are called the outer planets, these include: - Jupiter - Largest planet - Saturn - Second largest planet - Uranus - Neptune - These four are called Jovian or Gas Giant planets - Jovian means jupiter-like - Most of them are much larger than the terrestrial planets and have thick atmosphere, mostly of helium and hydrogen - Exoplanets - These are planets that orbit stars other than our Sun, making them "extrasolar" or "outside our solar system". They can be gas giants, rocky planets, or even icy planets. - Differences in composition - Why are the inner planets rocky while others are mostly in gaseous form? - The difference between terrestrial and jovian planets can be attributed to the following conditions: - The terrestrial planets have composition of rocks, metals, and other heavy elements which solidify while jovian planets are mainly formed of gaseous elements like hydrogen, helium, etc which don't solidify - The max pressure at jupiter's core forms metal hydrogen, in which hydrogen atoms are so close that electrons flow freely for one to another, a unique state - The terrestrial planets were formed in the close vicinity [surrounding area] of the parent star where it was too warm for gases to condense [become dense] to solid particles - Which means that only rocky and metallic materials (with higher melting points) could condense and form solid bodies in close vicinity. - Jovian planets were formed at quite a distant [far away] location - The solar wind was most intense nearer the sun; so, it blew off lots of gas and dust from the terrestrial planets - The solar winds were not all that intense to cause similar removal of gases from the Jovian planets - The terrestrial planets are smaller and their lower gravity could not hold the escaping gases - Case of pluto - Till recently (August 2006), Pluto was also considered a planet - However, in a meeting of the International Astronomical Union, a decision was taken that Pluto like other celestial objects (2003 UB313) discovered in recent past may be called ‘dwarf planet’ - IAU’s 3 Criteria for a Full Planet: 1. Orbits the Sun - Pluto does this. 2. Has enough mass to assume a nearly round shape (hydrostatic equilibrium) - Pluto is spherical. 3. Has cleared its orbit of other debris - Pluto fails here. - It has only approx. 7% times the mass of the rest of the material in its orbit (Earth has over 1000×). - Pluto is about 0.2% the mass of Earth and about 18% the mass of the Moon. - It’s not gravitationally dominant in its zone — it doesn’t "clear out" other objects like planets do. - Types of planets - - Some metrics for planets in solar system -

* Distance from the sun in astronomical unit i.e. average mean distance of the earth is 149,598,000 km = 1 @ Density in gm/cm3 # Radius: Equatorial radius 6378.137 km = 1 - Asteroid belt - The asteroid belt is a region in the Solar System, located between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, where millions of asteroids orbit the Sun. - NEA (Near-Earth Asteroid) - NEA, short for Near-Earth Asteroid, refers to asteroids whose orbits bring them close to Earth's orbit. - Trojan asteroids are asteroids that share the orbit of a planet, but stay either ahead or behind it, typically at Lagrange points L4 or L5. - They are gravitationally stable in these positions and are thought to be remnants of the primordial material that formed the outer planets. - The best-known examples are the Jupiter Trojans, which orbit alongside Jupiter. - Kuiper belt - A region of the solar system beyond the orbit of Neptune, believed to contain many comets, asteroids, and other small bodies made largely of ice. - There are four known dwarf planets in the Kuiper belt viz. [namely / in other words] Pluto, Makemake, Haumea, and Eris - Earth and it's evolution - Initial state - Overview - Do you know that the planet earth initially was a barren, rocky and hot object with a thin atmosphere of hydrogen and helium - This is far from the present day picture of the earth - Hence, there must have been some events– processes, which may have caused this change from rocky, barren and hot earth to a beautiful planet with ample amount of water and conducive atmosphere favouring the existence of life - In the following section, you will find out how the period, between the 4,600 million years and the present, led to the evolution of life on the surface of the planet - Layered structure - The earth has a layered structure - From the outermost end of the atmosphere to the centre of the earth, the material that exists is not uniform - The atmospheric matter has the least density - From the surface to deeper depths, the earth’s interior has different zones and each of these contains materials with different characteristics - Evolution of lithosphere - Process of formation - How was the layered structure of the earth developed? - The earth was mostly in a volatile state during its primordial [existing at or from beginning of time] stage - Due to gradual increase in density the temperature inside has increased - As a result the material inside started getting separated depending on their densities - This allowed heavier materials (like iron) to sink towards the centre of the earth and the lighter ones to move towards the surface - With passage of time it cooled further and solidified and condensed into a smaller size - This later led to the development of the outer surface in the form of a crust - During the formation of the moon, due to the giant impact, the earth was further heated up - It is through the process of differentiation that the earth forming material got separated into different layers - Starting from the surface to the central parts, we have layers like the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core - From the crust to the core, the density of the material increases - We shall discuss in detail the properties of each of this layer in the next chapter - Evolution of atmosphere and hydrosphere - Current composition - The present composition of earth’s atmosphere is chiefly contributed by nitrogen and oxygen - You will be dealing with the composition and structure of the earth’s atmosphere in Chapter 8 - Stages of evolution - There are three stages in the evolution of the present atmosphere - The first stage is marked by the loss of primordial atmosphere - In the second stage, the hot interior of the earth contributed to the evolution of the atmosphere - Finally, the composition of the atmosphere was modified by the living world through the process of photosynthesis - Detailed process - The early atmosphere, with hydrogen and helium, is supposed to have been stripped off as a result of the solar winds - This happened not only in case of the earth, but also in all the terrestrial planets, which were supposed to have lost their primordial atmosphere through the impact of solar winds - During the cooling of the earth, gases and water vapour were released from the interior solid earth - This started the evolution of the present atmosphere - The early atmosphere largely contained water vapour, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and very little of free oxygen - The process through which the gases were outpoured from the interior is called degassing - Continuous volcanic eruptions contributed water vapour and gases to the atmosphere - As the earth cooled, the water vapour released started getting condensed - The carbon dioxide in the atmosphere got dissolved in rainwater and the temperature further decreased causing more condensation and more rains - The rainwater falling onto the surface got collected in the depressions to give rise to oceans - The earth’s oceans were formed within 500 million years from the formation of the earth - This tells us that the oceans are as old as 4,000 million years - Sometime around 3,800 million years ago, life began to evolve - However, around 2,500-3,000 million years before the present, the process of photosynthesis got evolved - Life was confined to the oceans for a long time - Oceans began to have the contribution of oxygen through the process of photosynthesis - Eventually, oceans were saturated [thoroughly soaked] with oxygen, and 2,000 million years ago, oxygen began to flood the atmosphere - Origin of life - Initial conditions and process - The last phase in the evolution of the earth relates to the origin and evolution of life - It is undoubtedly clear that initially the earth or even the atmosphere of the earth was not conducive [good for] for the development of life - Modern scientists refer to the origin of life as a kind of chemical reaction, which first generated complex organic molecules and assembled them - This assemblage was such that they could duplicate themselves converting inanimate matter into living substance - Evidence and timeline - The record of life that existed on this planet in different periods is found in rocks in the form of fossils - The microscopic structures closely related to the present form of blue algae have been found in geological formations much older than some 3,000 million years - It can be assumed that life began to evolve sometime 3,800 million years ago - The summary of evolution of life from unicellular bacteria to the modern man is given in the Geological Time Scale on page 18 - - Basics of geography - Latitudes and Longitudes - - Latitude (Horizontal Lines) - Latitude is a geographic coordinate that measures the distance of a location on Earth from the Equator. - An imaginary line notionally drawn on the earth equidistant from the poles, dividing the earth into northern and southern hemispheres and constituting the parallel of latitude 0° - It is measured with 180 imaginary lines known as parallels. - All parallels north of the equator are called ‘north latitudes.’ Similarly all parallels south of the equator are called ‘south latitudes.’ - Each parallel measures one degree north or south of the Equator and 90 degrees north of the Equator and 90 degrees south of the Equator. - One degree degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers. - Run east–west, but measure positions north or south of the Equator. - By measuring the angle of the Pole Star from your place, you can know the latitude of your place. - The Equator is 0° latitude. - The upper hemisphere is called Northern Hemisphere. - The lower hemisphere is called Souther Hemisphere. - Values range from 0° to 90°: - North of Equator: 0° to 90°N (e.g., New Delhi is ~28.6°N) - South of Equator: 0° to 90°S (e.g., Sydney is ~33.9°S) - Key Latitudes: - Equator (0°) - Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) - Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S) - Arctic Circle (66.5°N) - Antarctic Circle (66.5°S) - Heat zones according to greeks -Torrid zone (Hottest areas) - Area between tropic of cancer and tropic of capricorn. - Temperate zone (misnomer for Moderate areas) - North temperate zone - Area between tropic of cancer and arctic circle. - South temperate zone - Area between tropic of capricorn and antarctic circle. - Frigid zone (coldest areas) - Areas at north and south pole. - Longitude (Vertical Lines) - Longitude is the measurement east or west of the prime meridian. Run north–south, but measure positions east or west of the Prime Meridian. - Longitude is measured by imaginary lines that run around Earth vertically and meet at the North and South Poles. These lines are known as meridians. - Unlike parallels of latitude, all meridians are of equal length but they are not parallel like latitudes - A degree of longitude is about 111 kilometers at its widest. - The widest areas of longitude are near the Equator, where Earth bulges out. - All meridians meet and north and south poles. - Prime meridian - The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) passes through Greenwich, England. - Its value is 0° longitude and from it we count 180° eastward as well as 180° westward - Values range from 0° to 180°: - East of Greenwich: 0° to 180°E (e.g., India is ~77°E) - West of Greenwich: 0° to 180°W (e.g., New York is ~74°W) - Longitude and time - - The world has been divided into 24 major time zones of one hour each. Each zone thus covers 15° of longitude. - The Prime meridian is taken as the point of reference for calculating time. The time measured at the Prime Medidian is called the Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). - As the earth rotates from west to east, those places east of Greenwich are ahead of the GMT and those to the west are behind it. - The earth rotates 360 degree in about 24 hours, it takes 4 minutes to cover 1 degree longitude. - Thus, when it is 12 noon at Greenwich, the time at 15° east of Greenwich will be 15 × 4 = 60 minutes, i.e., 1 hour ahead of Greenwich time, which means 1 p.m. - But at 15° west of Greenwich, the time will be behind Greenwich time by one hour, - Why do we have standard time? - The local time of places which are on different meridians are bound to differ and create chaos related to time bound tasks and management. - It is, therefore, necessary to adopt the local time of some central meridian of a country as the standard time for the country. - In India, the longitude of 82½° E (82° 30'E) is treated as the standard meridian. - The local time at this meridian is taken as the standard time for the whole country. - It is known as the Indian Standard Time (IST). - Large countries like Russia Canada and the United States have vast longitudinal extent. They do not have a single Standard Time for the whole Country - Daylight Saving Time - Daylight Saving Time, system for uniformly advancing clocks, so as to extend daylight hours during conventional waking time in the summer months - It is practices in countries which are at extreme north and south. - Reason - Better use of daytime - Saves energy as use of artifical lighting is lessened. - Motion of the Earth - Rotation - - Earth's rotation, also known as Earth's spin, is the planet's circular movement around its own axis. - This rotation takes approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds to complete and is responsible for the cycle of day and night. Earth rotates eastward, counterclockwise when viewed from above the North Pole. - Solar day vs sidereal day - - Solar Day (24 hours) – What We Use Daily - The time the Earth takes to face the Sun again at the same position (e.g., noon to noon). - It includes the Earth’s rotation plus a little extra to catch up with the Sun, because the Earth is also moving around the Sun. - This is the 24-hour day on your clock. - The period of rotation is known as the earth day - Sidereal Day (23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds) – Actual Rotation Time - The time Earth takes to complete one full 360° spin relative to distant stars. - It’s shorter because while the Earth spins, it also moves forward in its orbit, so it needs to rotate a bit more to face the Sun again. - This is used in astronomy and satellite tracking. - Significance of earth's rotation - - Day and Night Cycle (Diurnal cycle) - The most direct effect of Earth's rotation is the alternation of day and night. - As Earth rotates from west to east, different parts face the Sun (day) while others are in shadow (night), enabling a 24-hour time cycle that regulates biological rhythms (circadian rhythms) in plants, animals, and humans. - Circle of illumination - The circle which divides day area vs night area of earth is called circle of illumination. - - Coriolis Effect - The rotation causes the Coriolis force, which deflects the path of moving air and water: - To the right in the Northern Hemisphere (near earth's surface) - To the left in the Southern Hemisphere (near earth's surface) - How it works: - The Earth rotates from west to east. - Because of this rotation, different parts of the Earth move at different speeds: - At the equator, the surface is moving fastest (~1670 km/h). - At the poles, it's almost not moving at all. - This is essential for the formation of weather patterns, ocean currents, and cyclones. - Effect and deviations at higher altitudes - The air rising near the equator moves poleward at high altitudes (around the tropopause). - This poleward moving air at high altitude is moving into regions of faster rotation (because the Earth’s surface velocity is higher at the equator). - Due to conservation of angular momentum, as air moves poleward it gains an eastward velocity relative to the surface. - This results in strong westerly winds aloft (blowing from west to east). - These are called westerly jet streams — such as the subtropical jet and polar jet. - Why doesn’t angular momentum act on air moving from poles to equator near the surface? - Air near the surface moves from high pressure (poles) to low pressure (equator), but its initial eastward velocity near the poles is low because Earth’s surface speed near the poles is slow (smaller circumference of latitude circles). - As the air moves towards the equator near the surface, it moves into regions where the Earth’s surface speed is faster. - But because it’s near the surface, friction with the ground slows it down a lot, so it doesn’t speed up to match the faster rotating surface at the equator. - This causes the air to lag behind the surface rotation and therefore the Coriolis force acts to deflect it westward (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere). - Time Zones - Because of rotation, different longitudes experience sunrise and sunset at different times. - The Earth is divided into 24 time zones, roughly 15° of longitude apart, with each zone representing one hour. - Flattening at the Poles - Earth's rotation causes a centrifugal force, making it slightly bulge at the equator and flatten at the poles. - This makes Earth an oblate spheroid, not a perfect sphere. - Tidal Effects (Minor) - While tides are mainly due to the Moon and Sun's gravity, Earth's rotation influences the timing and frequency of tides. - Influence on Satellites and Navigation - Earth’s rotation is crucial for launching and tracking satellites. - Navigation systems (like GPS) must account for Earth's rotation to provide accurate positioning. - Revolution - - The revolution of Earth refers to its yearly journey around the Sun in a fixed, elliptical path. - This movement takes approximately 365.25 days to complete, which is why we have leap years every four years to account for the extra quarter of a day. - The day is added to only February because of some old Roman thing and people just continued with that in modern times. - The Earth revolves at varying speeds, reaching its fastest point when closest to the Sun (perihelion) and its slowest when farthest away (aphelion). - Farthest and nearest points in earth's object - Aphelion - It is the point in a celestial body's orbit where it is farthest from the Sun. Earth's aphelion occurs in early July, around July 3rd or 4th, at which time it's about 152.1 million kilometers from the Sun. - This is about 4.8 million kilometers farther than Earth's perihelion. - Perihelion - The point in the orbit of a planet, asteroid, or comet at which it is closest to the sun. Earth's perihelion occurs around January 3rd. - Significance of earth's revolution - Formation of Seasons - Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5° relative to its orbital plane. - The plane formed by the orbit is known as the orbital plane - As it revolves around the Sun, different parts of Earth receive varying amounts of sunlight throughout the year. - Summer occurs when a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. - Winter occurs when it is tilted away. - This variation causes spring, summer, autumn, and winter, each with distinct climate and ecological impacts. - Variation in Day Length - Due to revolution and axial tilt, day length changes over the year: - Longer days in summer - Shorter days in winter - This affects plant growth, animal behavior, and human activities. - Temperature Changes - Revolution leads to solar energy distribution changes across the globe over the year. - Areas receive more direct sunlight in summer, increasing temperatures, and less in winter, lowering them. - Annual Cycle of Life - Many biological processes (like flowering, migration, hibernation) are tied to seasonal changes caused by Earth’s revolution. - Agriculture relies heavily on these cycles — sowing, growing, and harvesting are season-dependent. - Determination of a Year - One complete revolution takes about 365.25 days, which defines a calendar year. - The extra 0.25 day leads to a leap year every four years. - Geographic and magnetic poles - - Geographic Poles - The Geographic poles refer to the two fixed points where the Earth's axis of rotation intersects its surface. - These are the North Pole and South Pole: - North Pole: Located at 90°N latitude, at the northernmost point of Earth's axis. - South Pole: Located at 90°S latitude, at the southernmost point of Earth's axis. - The Geographic poles are fixed in position, meaning they do not move over time. - Magnetic Poles - The Magnetic poles are the points where the Earth's magnetic field is vertical. - There are two magnetic poles: - North Magnetic Pole: Located in the northern hemisphere (currently shifting toward Russia). - South Magnetic Pole: Located near Antarctica. - Unlike the Geographic poles, Magnetic poles are not fixed and move over time due to changes in the Earth's magnetic field (due to fluid motions in the outer core). - Key Differences: - Geographic poles: Fixed, determined by Earth's rotation axis. - Magnetic poles: Move, determined by Earth's magnetic field. - Various terms - Declination angle - The angle between true North and magnetic North at any particular position. - Pole reversal - Complete reversal of the magnetic poles of the earth over several thousands of years. - This occurs over thousands of years due to changes in the convection patterns within Earth's outer core, where the magnetic field is generated. - Magnetosphere - The magnetosphere is the region of space around Earth that is controlled by Earth's magnetic field. - It extends several thousand kilometers into space, protecting Earth from harmful solar wind and cosmic radiation. - It is shaped by the interaction of the solar wind with Earth's magnetic field. - Magnetopause - The magnetopause is the boundary between Earth's magnetosphere and the solar wind. - It represents the point of pressure balance between the Earth's magnetic field and the incoming solar wind. - It is an abrupt boundary where the solar wind’s force is countered by the magnetic field’s pressure. - The distance from Earth varies depending on solar wind strength, but typically lies about 10 Earth radii from Earth. - Magnetosheath - The magnetosheath is the turbulent region of space just outside the magnetopause. - It is where the solar wind is slowed down and compressed as it encounters Earth's magnetic field. - The particles in the magnetosheath are deflected and can create phenomena such as auroras and geomagnetic storms. - Significance of Magnetosphere - The magnetosphere plays a crucial role in protecting life on Earth from solar radiation and cosmic rays. It deflects harmful charged particles away from the planet’s surface. - It also helps preserve the atmosphere by preventing the stripping away of atmospheric particles by solar winds, which could otherwise lead to atmospheric loss. - The magnetosphere’s interaction with solar winds leads to auroras (Northern and Southern Lights), which are both beautiful and a result of the magnetic field’s protection. - Seasons of earth - - The Earth’s tilt (23.5°) and revolution around the Sun cause seasonal changes, marked by two solstices and two equinoxes each year. - Summer Solstice - Date: Around June 21 - Position: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. - Sun’s vertical rays fall on: Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) - Significance: - Longest day and shortest night in the Northern Hemisphere. - Marks the start of summer in the Northern Hemisphere. - Opposite in the Southern Hemisphere (they experience winter). - Winter Solstice - Date: Around December 21 - Position: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. - Sun’s vertical rays fall on: Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S) - Significance: - Shortest day and longest night in the Northern Hemisphere. - Marks the start of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. - Opposite in the Southern Hemisphere (they experience summer). - Vernal Equinox (Spring Equinox) - Date: Around March 21 - Sun’s vertical rays fall on: Equator (0°) - Position: Neither hemisphere is tilted toward or away from the Sun. - Significance: - Day and night are equal (12 hours each) everywhere on Earth. - Marks the start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere. - Start of autumn in the Southern Hemisphere. - Autumnal Equinox (Fall Equinox) - Date: Around September 23 - Sun’s vertical rays fall on: Equator (0°) - Position: Again, no tilt toward or away. - Significance: - Equal day and night worldwide. - Marks the start of autumn in the Northern Hemisphere. - Start of spring in the Southern Hemisphere. - Maps, sketch and plan - Map - A map is a representation or drawing of the Earth's surface or a part of it on a flat surface, drawn according to a scale. It provides detailed information about various features and locations. - Types of Maps - Physical Maps: - Show natural features like mountains, plateaus, plains, rivers, and oceans. - Political Maps: - Depict cities, towns, villages, countries, and states with their boundaries. - Thematic Maps: - Focus on specific information such as road networks, rainfall distribution, forests, industries, etc. - Components of Maps - Distance: - Maps use a scale to represent the ratio between actual distances on the ground and distances on the map. - Large Scale Maps: Show small areas in greater detail (e.g., a village map). - Small Scale Maps: Cover large areas with less detail (e.g., a world map). - Direction: - Maps indicate directions with a compass rose or an arrow pointing north. - Cardinal Directions (Cardinal points): North, South, East, West. - Intermediate Directions: North-East (NE), South-East (SE), South-West (SW), North-West (NW). - Symbols: - Standard symbols represent features like buildings, roads, bridges, etc. - Conventional Symbols: Universally accepted symbols used for easy understanding. - Colour Conventions: - Blue: Water bodies. - Brown: Mountains. - Yellow: Plateaus. - Green: Plains. - Sketch: - A rough drawing based on memory and observation, not to scale. - Used to show directions or locations informally. - Plan: - A detailed drawing of a small area on a large scale. - Provides exact measurements and is used for specific purposes like building layouts. - Major Domains of the Earth - The earth is made up of four major domains — Lithosphere, Hydrosphere, Atmosphere, and Biosphere — that are closely interconnected and support life. - Domains in detail - Lithosphere (Land) - Definition: - The solid, outermost layer of the Earth, made up of rocks and soil. - Continents: Asia - Largest continent by both area and population. - Covers ~30% of the Earth’s total land area and houses ~60% of the world population. - Bounded by the Arctic Ocean (north), Pacific Ocean (east), Indian Ocean (south), and Europe (west). - Features the world’s highest point — Mount Everest (8,848 m). - Origin of major ancient civilizations — Indus Valley, Mesopotamia, Chinese. - Extremely diverse in culture, languages, climates, and geography. - Home to vast deserts (Gobi, Thar), massive rivers (Yangtze, Ganga), and dense rainforests (Southeast Asia). - Africa - Second-largest continent. - Only continent to be crossed by the Equator, Tropic of Cancer, and Tropic of Capricorn — lies in all four hemispheres. - Rich in mineral resources and biodiversity (e.g., Congo Rainforest, Sahara Desert). - Bounded by the Mediterranean Sea (north), Indian Ocean (east), Atlantic Ocean (west). - Birthplace of humanity — earliest human fossils found in the Great Rift Valley. - Major rivers: Nile (longest), Congo, Niger. - Contains vast deserts (Sahara) and savannas. - North America - Third-largest continent. - Bounded by Arctic Ocean (north), Atlantic Ocean (east), Pacific Ocean (west), and South America (south). - Dominated by varied geography — Rocky Mountains, Great Plains, Great Lakes. - Includes high-income nations like the USA and Canada and developing nations in Central America. - Features important river systems like Mississippi and Missouri. - Home to the Grand Canyon and diverse climates — tundra in the north, tropical in the south. - South America - Lies mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. - Home to the Amazon Rainforest and Amazon River (largest by volume). - Bounded by the Atlantic (east) and Pacific (west) Oceans. - Dominated by the Andes Mountains (longest continental mountain range). - Rich in biodiversity and natural resources — forests, minerals, oil. - Inhabited by ancient civilizations like the Inca. - Contains deserts (Atacama), grasslands (Pampas), and wetlands (Pantanal). - Antarctica - Lies entirely in the Southern Hemisphere, encircling the South Pole. - Covered almost entirely by ice — 90% of Earth’s freshwater locked in ice sheets. - Coldest, driest, and windiest continent. - No permanent human residents, only scientific research stations. - Rich in marine biodiversity — krill, seals, penguins. - Plays a key role in regulating Earth’s climate and ocean currents. - Europe - Smallest continent after Australia by area. - Lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere. - Shares landmass with Asia — the two form Eurasia (divided by Ural Mountains). - Bounded by Arctic Ocean (north), Atlantic Ocean (west), and Mediterranean Sea (south). - Cradle of Western civilization — Greek, Roman, Renaissance periods. - Highly developed and urbanized — dense rail and road networks. - Important rivers: Danube, Rhine, Volga. - Australia (Oceania) - Smallest continent but largest island. - Lies entirely in the Southern Hemisphere. - Geographically isolated — unique flora and fauna (kangaroo, koala, eucalyptus). - Surrounded by the Indian and Pacific Oceans. - Flat and arid — most of the population lives along the coasts. - Home to the Great Barrier Reef, world’s largest coral reef system. - Includes nearby Pacific islands (Fiji, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand) in the Oceania region. - Landforms: - Mountains, plateaus, plains, valleys, deserts, etc. - Hydrosphere (Water) - Definition: - All the water on Earth — oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, glaciers, and underground water. - Water covers about 71% of the Earth’s surface. - Oceans: - Pacific Ocean - Largest and deepest ocean. - Covers ~63 million square miles. - Contains the Mariana Trench (deepest point on Earth). - Bounded by Asia, Australia, North and South America. - High tectonic activity (Ring of Fire). - Atlantic Ocean - Second-largest ocean. - Has the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (submarine mountain range). - Key for transatlantic trade and colonization history. - Separated by the Americas on the west and Europe-Africa on the east. - Indian Ocean - Third-largest ocean. - Warmest ocean among all. - Bounded by Asia (north), Africa (west), and Australia (east). - Plays a crucial role in the Indian Monsoon. - Important shipping lanes and strategic chokepoints (e.g., Strait of Hormuz, Malacca). - Southern (Antarctic) Ocean - Encircles Antarctica. - Officially recognized in 2000. - Connects Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans. - Drives global thermohaline circulation due to cold, dense water masses. - Arctic Ocean - Smallest and shallowest. - Mostly ice-covered throughout the year. - Bordered by North America, Europe, and Asia. - Strategic importance increasing due to melting ice and new shipping routes. - Atmosphere (Air) - Definition: - The blanket of gases surrounding the Earth. - Provides oxygen, protects from harmful solar radiation, and maintains temperature. - Main Gases: - Nitrogen (78%) - Oxygen (21%) - Others: - Carbon dioxide, Argon, Ozone, etc. - Layers of Atmosphere (mentioned briefly): - Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere. - Biosphere (Life) - Definition: - The narrow zone where land, water, and air interact to support life. - Includes all living organisms — plants, animals, humans, and microorganisms. - The biosphere depends on balance among lithosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. - Interdependence of Domains - Life (biosphere) exists because of the interaction of the other three domains. - Example: Plants (biosphere) need sunlight (atmosphere), water (hydrosphere), and soil (lithosphere). - Human activities affect all domains — e.g., deforestation, pollution, global warming.

Section: Geomorphology

- Interior of the earth - Introduction to the earth's interior - Questions and imagery - What do you imagine about the nature of the earth? - Do you imagine it to be a solid ball like cricket ball or a hollow ball with a thick cover of rocks i.e. lithosphere? - Have you ever seen photographs or images of a volcanic eruption on the television screen? - Can you recollect [remember] the emergence [appearance / arrival] of hot molten lava, dust, smoke, fire and magma flowing out of the volcanic crater? - Importance and limitations - The interior of the earth can be understood only by indirect evidences as neither any one has nor any one can reach the interior of the earth - The configuration [arrangement of parts or elements in a particular form] of the surface of the earth is largely a product of the processes operating in the interior of the earth - Exogenic [formed or occurring on the surface of the earth] as well as endogenic [formed or occurring beneath the surface of the earth] processes are constantly shaping the landscape - A proper understanding of the physiographic character of a region remains incomplete if the effects of endogenic processes are ignored - Human life is largely influenced by the physiography (physical geography) of the region - Therefore, it is necessary that one gets acquainted [familiar] with the forces that influence landscape development - To understand why the earth shakes or how a tsunami wave is generated, it is necessary that we know certain details of the interior of the earth - Context and focus - In the previous chapter, you have noted that the earth-forming materials have been distributed in the form of layers from the crust to the core - It is interesting to know how scientists have gathered information about these layers and what are the characteristics of each of these layers - This is exactly what this chapter deals with - Sources of information about the interior - Overview - General constraints - The earth’s radius is 6,370 km - No one can reach the centre of the earth and make observations or collect samples of the material - Under such conditions, you may wonder how scientists tell us about the earth’s interior and the type of materials that exist at such depths - Most of our knowledge about the interior of the earth is largely based on estimates and inferences [deduction / conclusion / reasoning] - Yet, a part of the information is obtained through direct observations and analysis of materials - Direct sources - Surface rocks - The most easily available solid earth material is surface rocks. - Mining and drilling projects - Mining - These include the rocks and materials from mining areas. - Gold mines in South Africa are as deep as 3 - 4 km. - Going beyond [on further side of] this depth is not possible as it is very hot at this depth. - Drilling - Besides mining, scientists have taken up a number of projects to penetrate deeper depths to explore the conditions in the crustal [relating to or originating in the earth's crust] portions. - Scientists world over are working on two major projects such as “Deep Ocean Drilling Project” and “Integrated Ocean Drilling Project”. - The deepest drill at Kola, in Arctic Ocean, has so far reached a depth of 12 km. - This and many deep drilling projects have provided large volume of information through the analysis of materials collected at different depths. - Volcanism - Volcanic eruption forms another source of obtaining direct information - As and when the molten material (magma) is thrown onto the surface of the earth, during volcanic eruption it becomes available for laboratory analysis - However, it is difficult to ascertain [make sure / find out] the depth of the source of such magma - Indirect sources - Physical properties - Analysis of properties of matter indirectly provides information about the interior - We know through the mining activity that temperature and pressure increase with the increasing distance from the surface towards the interior in deeper depths - Pressure increases with depth because of the weight of all the material above pressing down due to gravity. - Temperature increases as a lot of heat is trapped inside, slowly escaping over billions of years. - Heat sources of earth - Primordial Heat (leftover from Earth's formation): - 30% to 50% of Earth's current heat. - Gradually decreasing over time. - Radioactive Decay (from elements like uranium, thorium, and potassium): - 50% to 70% of Earth's current heat. - This source is constant and continues to generate heat. - Other Sources (like tidal heating from the Moon and friction within Earth's layers): - A very small percentage (less than 5%). - Moreover, it is also known that the density of the material also increases with depth - It is possible to find the rate of change of these characteristics - Knowing the total thickness of the earth, scientists have estimated the values of temperature, pressure and the density of materials at different depths - The details of these characteristics with reference to each layer of the interior are discussed later in this chapter - Meteors - Another source of information are the meteors that at times reach the earth - However, it may be noted that the material that becomes available for analysis from meteors, is not from the interior of the earth - The material and the structure observed in the meteors are similar to that of the earth - They are solid bodies developed out of materials same as, or similar to, our planet - Hence, this becomes yet another source of information about the interior of the earth - Geophysical methods - The other indirect sources include gravitation, magnetic field, and seismic activity - Gravitation - The gravitation force (g) is not the same at different latitudes on the surface - It is greater near the poles and less at the equator - This is because of the distance from the centre at the equator being greater than that at the poles - The gravity values also differ according to the mass of material - The uneven distribution of mass of material within the earth influences this value - The reading of the gravity at different places is influenced by many other factors - These readings differ from the expected values - Such a difference is called gravity anomaly [abnormality / irregularity / inconsistency] - Gravity anomalies give us information about the distribution of mass of the material in the crust of the earth - Magnetic field - Magnetic surveys also provide information about the distribution of magnetic materials in the crustal portion, and thus, provide information about the distribution of materials in this part - Seismic activity - Seismic activity is one of the most important sources of information about the interior of the earth - Hence, we shall discuss it in some detail - Structure of the earth - - - Layers - The crust - It is the outermost solid part of the earth - It is brittle in nature - The thickness of the crust varies under the oceanic and continental areas - Oceanic crust is thinner as compared to the continental crust - It constituent less than 1% of earths mass and volume. - Composition of crust - - Divisions - Continental crust (SIAL) - It is thicker than oceanic crust - The continental crust is thicker in the areas of major mountain systems - It is as much as 70 km thick in the Himalayan region - The mean thickness of the continental crust is around 30 km - Rich in lighter elements like silicon, aluminium, potassium, and sodium. - Less dense (average density ~2.7 g/cm³) compared to oceanic crust - Mainly made of granitic rocks - Mainly made from from SIAL (Silica and Aluminum) - Oceanic crust (SIMA) - It is thinner than continent crust - The mean thickness of oceanic crust is 5 km - Rich in heavier elements like magnesium and iron. - Denser (average density ~3.0 g/cm³) compared to continental crust. - Mainly made of basaltic rocks - Mainly made from SIMA (Silica and Magnesium) - The mantle - The portion of the interior beyond the crust is called the mantle - It extends from the Mohorovičić Discontinuity (Moho) to a depth of about 2,900 km. - It holds 67% of the earth's mass and 83% of earths volume. - Division - Lithosphere - Comprises the crust and the uppermost solid part of the mantle. - It is rigid and broken into tectonic plates. - Thickness ranges from 10 to 200 km. - Asthenosphere (Upper Mantle) - Located in the upper portion of the mantle. - Extends up to 400 km below the surface. - The term "astheno" means weak. - It is partially molten and behaves like a plastic solid. - It is the main source of magma that surfaces during volcanic eruptions. - Lower Mantle - Lies beneath the asthenosphere, extending to the core–mantle boundary. - It is in a solid state, though it can flow slowly over geological time. - The Core - The existence of the core was inferred through the study of earthquake wave velocities, which change significantly at certain depths. - The core–mantle boundary is located at a depth of approximately 2,900 km beneath the Earth's surface. - The core is composed primarily of heavy metals, mainly nickel and iron, and is therefore sometimes called the "NiFe layer" (Ni = Nickel, Fe = Iron). - It holds 33% of earth's mass and 16% of earths volume. - Division - Outer Core - Lies between the mantle and the inner core. - Extends from a depth of 2,900 km to about 5,150 km. - It is in a liquid state. - Responsible for generating Earth’s magnetic field due to the movement of molten metal. - The outer core is responsible for Earth's magnetic field through the geodynamo effect - The convection currents in the liquid outer core, combined with Earth’s rotation, create electric currents. - These electric currents generate a strong, dynamic magnetic field surrounding the Earth. - - Inner Core - Extends from a depth of about 5,150 km to 6,371 km (Earth's center). - It is in a solid state despite the high temperature, due to immense pressure. - Composed mainly of iron and nickel, and is extremely dense. - Inner core rotates slightly faster relative to the rotation of the surface. - The solid inner core is too hot to hold a permanent magnetic field, so outer core is mainly responsible for Earth's magnetic field. - Seismic Discontinuity - A seismic discontinuity is a boundary within the Earth where seismic wave velocity changes abruptly due to a change in material composition or state. These boundaries help scientists understand Earth’s internal layering. - - Major Seismic Discontinuities - Conrad Discontinuity - The Conrad Discontinuity is a boundary within the Earth's continental crust. - It separates the upper crust (less dense, granitic) from the lower crust (denser, basaltic). - Found at a depth of about 15–20 km beneath continents. - Not present under oceanic crust. - Mohorovičić Discontinuity (Moho) -Boundary between the crust and the mantle. -Discovered by Andrija Mohorovičić in 1909. -Seismic wave velocity increases sharply here. -Depth: ~35 km under continents, ~5–10 km under oceans. - Repetti Discontinuity - The Repetti Discontinuity lies within the mantle. - It separates the upper mantle from the lower mantle. - Located at a depth of around 1,000 km (though estimates vary between 800–1,200 km). - It is marked by a change in seismic wave velocities, indicating a change in mineral structure or composition. - Less distinct than the Moho, Gutenberg, or Lehmann discontinuities, but important in understanding mantle dynamics. - Gutenberg Discontinuity - Boundary between the mantle and the outer core. - Discovered by Beno Gutenberg. - Located at a depth of ~2,900 km. - S-waves disappear here, indicating the liquid nature of the outer core. - Lehmann Discontinuity - Boundary between the outer core and the inner core. - Discovered by Inge Lehmann. - Located at ~5,150 km depth. - Marks the transition from liquid outer core to solid inner core. - Earthquakes and volcanism - Earthquake - Definition and overview - The study of seismic waves provides a complete picture of the layered interior - An earthquake in simple words is shaking of the earth - It is a natural event - It is caused due to release of energy, which generates waves that travel in all directions - Why does the earth shake? - Mechanism - The release of energy occurs along a fault - A fault is a sharp break in the crustal rocks - Rocks along a fault tend to move in opposite directions - As the overlying rock strata [layer of rocks] press them, the friction locks them together - However, their tendency to move apart at some point of time overcomes the friction - As a result, the blocks get deformed and eventually, they slide past one another abruptly [suddenly and unexpectedly] - This causes a release of energy, and the energy waves travel in all directions - Key locations - Focus / hypocenter - The point where the energy is released is called the focus of an earthquake, alternatively, it is called the hypocenter - The hypocenter can be divided into three types on the basis of depth 1. Shallow focus - Depth ranging from 0 km to - 70 km 2. Intermediate focus - Depth ranging from 70 km to - 300 km 3, Deep focus - Depth ranging from 300 km to - 700 km - Epicenter - The energy waves traveling in different directions reach the surface - The point on the surface, nearest to the focus, is called epicenter - It is the first one to experience the waves - It is a point directly above the focus - Types of earthquakes - On the basis of depth of the focus/hypocenter - Shallow earthquake - Shallow hypocenter (0-70 km) - Intermediate earthquake - Intermediate hypocenter (70-300 km) - Deep earthquake - Deep hypocenter (300-700 km) - On the basis of causality - - Tectonic earthquakes - These are generated due to sliding of rocks along a fault plane - Volcanic earthquake - These are caused by slip on a fault near a volcano - Collapse causing minor tremors - In the areas of intense mining activity, sometimes the roofs of underground mines collapse - These are called collapse earthquakes - Explosion earthquake - Ground shaking may also occur due to the explosion of chemical or nuclear devices - Such tremors are called explosion earthquakes - Reservoir Induced earthquakes - The earthquakes that occur in the areas of large reservoirs [large water body] are referred to as reservoir induced earthquakes - Earthquake waves and their characteristics - - General characteristics - All natural earthquakes take place in the lithosphere - It is sufficient [enough] to note here that the lithosphere refers to the portion of depth up to 200 km from the surface of the earth - Seismograph / seismometer - An instrument called ‘seismograph’ records the waves reaching the surface - A curve of earthquake waves recorded on the seismograph is given in Figure 3.1 - Note that the curve shows three distinct sections each representing different types of wave patterns - The velocity and direction of waves changes as they travel through materials with different densities - The denser the material, the higher is the velocity - Their direction changes as they reflect [send back] or refract [changing direction] when coming across materials with different densities - Reflection and refraction - Reflection causes waves to rebound whereas refraction makes waves move in different directions - The variations in the direction of waves are inferred with the help of their record on seismograph - Types of waves - Body waves - Body waves are generated due to the release of energy at the focus and move in all directions traveling through the body of the earth - Hence, the name body waves - There are two types of body waves - P-waves - P-waves move faster and are the first to arrive at the surface - These are also called ‘primary waves’ - The P-waves are similar to sound waves - Longitudinal (parallel motion). - They travel through gaseous, liquid and solid materials - P-waves slow down and refract in the outer core, confirming material change. - S-waves - S-waves arrive at the surface with some time lag - These are called secondary waves - Transverse (perpendicular motion). -
