Note that the subcontinent was still close to the equator - From 40 million years ago and thereafter, the event of formation of the Himalayas took place - Scientists believe that the process is still continuing and the height of the Himalayas is rising even to this date - Minerals and rocks - Introduction to minerals - Composition of the earth - The earth is composed of various kinds of elements - These elements are in solid form in the outer layer of the earth and in hot and molten form in the interior - About 98 per cent of the total crust of the earth is composed of eight elements like oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium, and the rest is constituted by titanium, hydrogen, phosphorous, manganese, sulphur, carbon, nickel and other elements - Definition of minerals - The elements in the earth’s crust are rarely found exclusively but are usually combined with other elements to make various substances - These substances are recognised as minerals - Thus, a mineral is a naturally occurring organic and inorganic substance, having an orderly atomic structure and a definite chemical composition and physical properties - A mineral is composed of two or more elements - But, sometimes single element minerals like sulphur, copper, silver, gold, graphite etc. are found - Variety and formation - Though the number of elements making up the lithosphere are limited they are combined in many different ways to make up many varieties of minerals - There are at least 2,000 minerals that have been named and identified in the earth crust; but almost all the commonly occurring ones are related to six major mineral groups that are known as major rock forming minerals - The basic source of all minerals is the hot magma in the interior of the earth - When magma cools, crystals of minerals appear and a systematic series of minerals are formed in sequence to solidify so as to form rocks - Minerals such as coal, petroleum and natural gas are organic substances found in solid, liquid and gaseous forms respectively - Physical characteristics - Overview - A brief information about some important minerals in terms of their nature and physical characteristics is given below - Characteristics - External crystal form — determined by internal arrangement of the molecules — cubes, octahedrons, hexagonal prisms, etc. - Cleavage — tendency to break in given directions producing relatively plane surfaces — result of internal arrangement of the molecules — may cleave in one or more directions and at any angle to each other - Fracture — internal molecular arrangement so complex there are no planes of molecules; the crystal will break in an irregular manner, not along planes of cleavage - Lustre — appearance of a material without regard to colour; each mineral has a distinctive lustre like metallic, silky, glossy etc. - Color — some minerals have characteristic colour determined by their molecular structure — malachite, azurite, chalcopyrite etc., and some minerals are coloured by impurities - For example, because of impurities quartz may be white, green, red, yellow etc. - Streak — colour of the ground powder of any mineral - It may be of the same colour as the mineral or may differ — malachite is green and gives green streak, fluorite is purple or green but gives a white streak - Transparency — transparent: light rays pass through so that objects can be seen plainly; translucent — light rays pass through but will get diffused so that objects cannot be seen; opaque — light will not pass at all - Structure — particular arrangement of the individual crystals; fine, medium or coarse grained; fibrous — separable, divergent, radiating - Hardness — relative resistance being scratched; ten minerals are selected to measure the degree of hardness from 1-10 - They are: 1. talc; 2. gypsum; 3. calcite; 4. fluorite; 5. apatite; 6. feldspar; 7. quartz; 8. topaz; 9. corundum; 10. diamond - Compared to this for example, a fingernail is 2.5 and glass or knife blade is 5.5 - Specific gravity — the ratio between the weight of a given object and the weight of an equal volume of water; object weighed in air and then weighed in water and divide weight in air by the difference of the two weights - Types of minerals - Metallic minerals - These minerals contain metal content and can be sub-divided into three types: 1. Precious metals: gold, silver, platinum etc. 2. Ferrous metals: iron and other metals often mixed with iron to form various kinds of steel 3. Non-ferrous metals: include metals like copper, lead, zinc, tin, aluminium etc. - Non-metallic minerals - These minerals do not contain metal content - Sulphur, phosphates and nitrates are examples of non-metallic minerals - Cement is a mixture of non-metallic minerals - Rocks - Definition and overview - The earth’s crust is composed of rocks - A rock is an aggregate [collection / cluster] of one or more minerals - Rock may be hard or soft and in varied colours - For example, granite is hard, soapstone is soft - Gabbro is black and quartzite can be milky white - Rocks do not have definite composition of mineral constituents - Feldspar and quartz are the most common minerals found in rocks - Petrology - Petrology is science of rocks - A petrologist studies rocks in all their aspects viz., mineral composition, texture, structure, origin, occurrence, alteration and relationship with other rocks - Importance for geographers - As there is a close relation between rocks and landforms, rocks and soils, a geographer requires basic knowledge of rocks - Classification of rocks - Overview - There are many different kinds of rocks which are grouped under three families on the basis of their mode of formation - They are: - Igneous Rocks — solidified from magma and lava; - Sedimentary Rocks — the result of deposition [action of depositing] of fragments of rocks by exogenous [external cause or origin] processes - Metamorphic Rocks — formed out of existing rocks undergoing recrystallization - - Igneous Rocks (Primary rocks) - Formation - Igneous rocks are known as primary rocks because they form directly from magma or lava - The word ‘igneous’ comes from the Latin word ignis, meaning ‘fire’ - These rocks are formed when molten magma cools and solidifies - The process of solidification can take place either beneath the earth’s surface (intrusive) or on the surface (extrusive) - When magma cools slowly beneath the surface, it forms intrusive igneous rocks - When lava erupts on the surface and cools rapidly, it forms extrusive igneous rocks - Classification of Igneous Rocks: - Based on Mode of Formation: - Intrusive (Plutonic) Rocks: - Formed from magma that cools and solidifies beneath the Earth's surface. - Slow cooling allows the formation of large, visible crystals (coarse-grained texture). - Examples: - Granite: Rich in quartz and feldspar, light-colored, coarse-grained. - Gabbro: Dark-colored, mafic composition, coarse-grained. - Pegmatite: Extremely coarse-grained, often with large crystals of quartz, feldspar, and mica. - Extrusive (Volcanic) Rocks: - Formed when magma (lava) erupts on the surface and cools rapidly. - Rapid cooling results in fine-grained or glassy texture with small or no visible crystals. - Examples: - Basalt: Dark-colored, fine-grained, rich in iron and magnesium. - Volcanic Breccia: Composed of angular rock fragments fused together during explosive eruptions. - Tuff: Formed from volcanic ash and dust compacted and cemented together. - Based on Texture (determined by cooling rate): - Coarse-Grained (Phaneritic): - Slow cooling deep inside the Earth. - Large, visible crystals. - Example: Granite, Gabbro. - Fine-Grained (Aphanitic): - Rapid cooling on or near the surface. - Small or no visible crystals. - Example: Basalt. - Very Coarse-Grained (Pegmatitic): - Extremely slow cooling or fluid-rich environments. - Exceptionally large crystals. - Example: Pegmatite. - Glassy: - Instant cooling with no time for crystal formation. - Example: Obsidian (not included above but good to note). - Porphyritic: - Two-stage cooling – large crystals (phenocrysts) embedded in a fine-grained matrix. - Indicates a complex cooling history. - Sedimentary Rocks - Formation - The word ‘sedimentary’ is derived from the Latin word sedimentum, meaning ‘settling’ - Rocks (igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic) at the earth’s surface undergo weathering and erosion due to denudational agents such as wind, water, and ice - The resulting fragments are transported and deposited by these agents - Over time, the accumulated deposits undergo compaction and cementation, turning into sedimentary rocks — a process called lithification - Sedimentary rocks often exhibit distinct layering or bedding, which can remain visible even after lithification - Common examples showing such layers include sandstone, shale, and limestone - Classification - Based on mode of formation, sedimentary rocks are classified into: 1. Mechanically formed - Formed by physical accumulation of rock fragments - Examples: sandstone, conglomerate, shale, loess 2. Organically formed - Formed from the accumulation of plant or animal remains - Examples: - From animals: chalk, coral limestone, some types of limestone - From plants: peat, lignite, bituminous coal 3. Chemically formed - Formed from mineral substances precipitated from solution - Examples: chert, gypsum, halite, potash, some types of limestone - Metamorphic rocks - Formation - The word metamorphic means ‘change of form’ - These rocks form under the action of pressure, volume and temperature (PVT) changes - Metamorphism occurs when rocks are forced down to lower levels by tectonic processes or when molten magma rising through the crust comes in contact with the crustal rocks or the underlying rocks are subjected to great amounts of pressure by overlying rocks - Metamorphism - Metamorphism is a process by which already consolidated rocks undergo recrystallisation and reorganisation of materials within original rocks - Types of Metamorphism - Dynamic Metamorphism - Caused primarily by mechanical forces such as crushing, grinding, and shearing - Occurs along fault zones where intense pressure leads to reorganization of minerals - No significant chemical changes take place - Example: Mylonites formed along fault zones - Thermal Metamorphism (also called Contact Metamorphism) - Occurs due to high temperatures from nearby intruding magma or lava - Recrystallisation of original rock minerals without much deformation - New minerals may also form due to the introduction of materials from magma/lava - Common near igneous intrusions - Regional Metamorphism - Caused by a combination of high pressure and temperature over large areas - Associated with tectonic plate collisions and mountain building - Rocks undergo deformation, chemical alteration, and recrystallisation - Produces foliated rocks like schist, gneiss - Structural Features of Metamorphic Rocks - Foliation - Refers to the alignment of mineral grains or structural features within a rock - Caused by pressure during metamorphism, leading to a layered or banded appearance - Lineation - Linear arrangement of minerals due to directed pressure - Common in rocks that have undergone significant deformation - Banding - Occurs when minerals segregate into alternating layers of light and dark shades - Rocks showing this structure are known as banded metamorphic rocks - Classification of Metamorphic Rocks - Based on Structure - Foliated Rocks - Exhibit parallel arrangement of minerals - Common examples: Slate, Schist, Gneiss - Non-Foliated Rocks - Do not show layered or banded texture - Usually composed of minerals that recrystallize without orientation [positioning / familiarization with something / a person's basic belief towards something] - Common examples: Marble (from limestone), Quartzite (from sandstone) - Based on Parent Rock (Protolith) - Slate: from shale (foliated) - Schist: from shale or basalt (foliated) - Gneiss: from granite or sedimentary rocks (foliated) - Marble: from limestone (non-foliated) - Quartzite: from sandstone (non-foliated) - Rock cycle - - Overview - Rocks do not remain in their original form for long but may undergo transformation - Rock cycle is a continuous process through which old rocks are transformed into new ones - Process - Igneous rocks are primary rocks and other rocks (sedimentary and metamorphic) form from these primary rocks - Igneous rocks can be changed into metamorphic rocks - The fragments derived out of igneous and metamorphic rocks form into sedimentary rocks - Sedimentary rocks themselves can turn into fragments and the fragments can be a source for formation of sedimentary rocks - The crustal rocks (igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary) once formed may be carried down into the mantle (interior of the earth) through subduction [sideways and downward movement of the edge of the plate beneath another plate] process (parts or whole of crustal plates going down under another plate in zones of plate convergence) and the same melt down due to increase in temperature in the interior and turn into molten magma, the original source for igneous rocks (Figure 5.1) - Landforms and their evolution - Introduction to landforms - Overview - After weathering processes have had their actions on the earth materials making up the surface of the earth, the geomorphic agents like running water, ground water, wind, glaciers, waves perform erosion - It is already known to you that erosion causes changes on the surface of the earth - Deposition follows erosion and because of deposition too, changes occur on the surface of the earth - Definition of landforms - A landform is a natural feature on the Earth's surface, like a mountain or a valley, that is shaped by geological processes like erosion, deposition, and tectonic activity - If landform is a small to medium sized part of the surface of the earth, what is a landscape [scenery]? - While a landform is a specific geomorphic feature like a hill, valley, or plateau, a landscape is the visible integration of multiple landforms and natural or man-made elements in a region, forming the overall appearance of that part of the Earth's surface. - Several related landforms together make up landscapes, (large tracts of earth’s surface) - Each landform has its own physical shape, size, materials and is a result of the action of certain geomorphic processes and agent(s) - Evolution of landforms - Actions of most of the geomorphic processes and agents are slow, and hence the results take a long time to take shape - Every landform has a beginning - Landforms once formed may change in their shape, size and nature slowly or fast due to continued action of geomorphic processes and agents - Due to changes in climatic conditions and vertical or horizontal movements of landmasses, either the intensity of processes or the processes themselves might change leading to new modifications in the landforms - Evolution here implies stages of transformation of either a part of the earth’s surface from one landform into another or transformation of individual landforms after they are once formed - That means, each and every landform has a history of development and changes through time - A landmass passes through stages of development somewhat comparable to the stages of life — youth, mature and old age - Mount everest is the highest landform and Mariana trench is the lowest - What are the two important aspects of the evolution of landforms? - Major Landforms of the Earth - - Mountains - A mountain is a natural elevation of the Earth's surface rising more prominently than a hill, usually with steep sides and significant exposed rock. - They are formed primarily due to endogenic forces such as tectonic activity and volcanism. - Characteristics: - Elevation is generally above 600 meters from the surrounding area - Exhibit prominent relief features - Often form major physical barriers and influence climate and biodiversity - Types of Mountains: - - Fold Mountains - Formed due to compressional forces resulting in the folding of rock strata - Most common and highest mountain ranges in the world - Young Fold Mountains: steep, rugged, seismically active - Examples: Himalayas, Andes, Rockies - Old Fold Mountains: worn down by erosion, lower in height - Examples: Aravallis, Urals, Appalachians - Block Mountains (Horst Mountains) - Formed due to tensional forces causing faulting in the Earth’s crust - A block is either uplifted (horst) or the surrounding land subsides (graben) - Typically have steep sides and flat tops - Examples: Sierra Nevada (USA), Vosges and Black Forest (Europe) - Volcanic Mountains - Formed by the accumulation of volcanic materials like lava, ash, and cinders - Built over time by repeated eruptions - Can be active, dormant, or extinct - Examples: Mount Fuji (Japan), Mount Kilimanjaro (Tanzania), Mount Mayon (Philippines) - Residual Mountains - Remnants of old mountains worn down by erosion - Also called erosional or denudational mountains - Usually isolated, rounded hills of hard rock - Examples: Aravallis (India), Nilgiris (India), Highlands of Scotland - Plateaus - A plateau is an extensive area of flat or gently undulating land that is significantly elevated above the surrounding terrain. - Plateaus are formed due to various geological processes such as uplift of land due to tectonic activity, volcanic eruptions, or erosion of surrounding areas. - Characteristics: - Elevated flat-topped landform with steep edges - May have rivers cutting deep gorges or canyons - Can be of volcanic, tectonic, or erosional origin - Often support human settlements, agriculture, and mineral extraction - Types of Plateaus: - Intermontane Plateaus (Tectonic Plateus) - Located between mountain ranges - Formed due to uplift during mountain building or by deposition of volcanic materials between ranges - Surrounded by mountains on all sides - Examples: Tibetan Plateau (between the Himalayas and Kunlun), Bolivian Plateau - Continental Plateaus (Uplifted Plateaus) - Located away from mountain ranges, often in the interior parts of continents - Formed due to broad tectonic uplift of large areas - Often bounded by steep escarpments on one or more sides - Examples: Deccan Plateau (India), Colorado Plateau (USA), Brazilian Highlands - Piedmont Plateaus - Located at the foot of mountain ranges - Formed by erosion or deposition at the base of mountains or through tectonic uplift - Transition zones between mountain regions and plains - Examples: Patagonian Plateau (Argentina), Appalachian Plateau (USA) - Volcanic Plateaus - Formed from successive lava flows spreading over large areas - Typically found in regions with prolonged volcanic activity - Examples: Antrim Plateau (Northern Ireland), Columbia Plateau (USA) - Dissected Plateaus - Originally flat plateaus that have been heavily eroded by rivers and streams - Rugged appearance due to deep valleys and gorges - Examples: Chotanagpur Plateau (India), Ozark Plateau (USA) - Plains - Plains are extensive, relatively flat or gently rolling areas of land with minimal elevation variation. - They are among the most fertile and densely populated landforms, suitable for agriculture, transport, and settlements. - Types of Plains: - Structural Plains - Formed by the uplift of horizontal or gently tilted sedimentary rock layers - Surfaces remain relatively undisturbed by folding or faulting - Typically found in continental interiors - Examples: Russian Plain (East European Plain), Great Plains (USA) - Depositional Plains - Formed by the deposition of sediments carried by rivers, glaciers, wind, or seas over time - Generally very fertile and flat - Subtypes: - Alluvial Plains: - Formed by rivers depositing alluvium - Example: Indo-Gangetic Plain (India) - Glacial Plains: - Formed by glacial deposits during and after ice ages - Example: Northern plains of Canada and northern USA - Coastal Plains: - Formed by marine sedimentation or emergence of sea floors - Example: Eastern Coastal Plains of India - Lacustrine Plains: - Formed by the drying up of lakes - Example: Kashmir Valley (India) - Erosional Plains - Formed by the gradual wearing down of elevated land by agents like rivers, glaciers, and wind - Features reduced relief and old, mature landscapes - Subtypes: - Peneplains: - Nearly level surfaces formed by prolonged erosion - Represent the final stage of fluvial erosion - Pediplains: - Formed in arid and semi-arid regions by wind and water erosion - Examples: West Central Australian Plain, parts of the Canadian Shield - Hills - Hills are natural elevations of the Earth's surface that are lower in height and more rounded than mountains. - They usually have gentle slopes and are found in a variety of landscapes, including near mountains or in isolated regions. - Hills are typically less than 600 meters (2,000 feet) above sea level. - Characteristics: - Smaller and lower than mountains - Rounded summit and gentle slopes - May form due to tectonic uplift, erosion, or volcanic activity - Types of Hills: - Residual Hills - Formed by the erosion of surrounding softer rocks, leaving behind more resistant rock - Example: Monadnocks in the USA, Inselbergs in Africa - Volcanic Hills - Formed by solidified lava or volcanic debris - Example: Hills in the Deccan Trap region (India) - Tectonic Hills - Result from minor folding, faulting, or uplift of the Earth’s crust - Example: Shillong Hills (Meghalaya, India) - Erosional Hills - Created through the long-term erosion of larger landforms - Example: Hills in the Eastern Ghats region - Examples: - Shillong Hills (India) - Eastern Ghats (India) - Nilgiri Hills (partly residual and erosional in origin) - Valleys - A valley is a low area of land between hills or mountains, typically with a river or stream running through it. Valleys are often formed through the process of erosion by water or glaciers. - Characteristics: - Lower elevation compared to the surrounding terrain - Often formed by river erosion or tectonic forces - Can be U-shaped (glacial valleys) or V-shaped (river valleys) - Typically contain rivers or streams, although some can be dry - Types of Valleys: - River Valleys - Formed by the erosional action of rivers or streams over long periods. - These valleys are typically V-shaped and are found in regions where rivers are active in erosion. - Example: Ganga Valley (India), Nile Valley (Egypt) - Rift Valleys - Formed due to tectonic forces, where the Earth's crust is pulled apart along faults, creating a deep, long, and often steep-sided valley. - Rift valleys can occur due to both continental and oceanic tectonic movements. - Example: Narmada Valley (India), East African Rift Valley (Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania) - Glacial Valleys - Formed by the movement of glaciers, which carve deep U-shaped valleys in mountainous regions. - These valleys typically have steep sides and flat floors. - Example: Yosemite Valley (USA), Kashmir Valley (India) - Structural Valleys - Formed by the differential erosion of rock layers, often due to folding or faulting. - These valleys have a structural origin and can exhibit unique geological features. - Example: The Rhone Valley (France), Suez Canal (Egypt) - Examples: - Ganga Valley (India) - Narmada Valley (India) - East African Rift Valley (Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania) - Kashmir Valley (India) - Deserts - A desert is a barren area of land where little precipitation occurs, resulting in a landscape of limited vegetation and often extreme temperature fluctuations. Deserts can be hot or cold and are typically characterized by arid conditions. - Characteristics: - Low annual rainfall (less than 250 mm per year) - Can be hot (e.g., Sahara, Thar) or cold (e.g., Gobi, Atacama) - Can feature sand dunes, gravel plains (regs), rocky surfaces (hamadas), or barren landscapes with little or no vegetation - Temperature extremes, with hot days and cold nights (or cold days and freezing nights in cold deserts) - Types of Deserts (based on surface features): - - Erg (Sand Desert) - Dominated by sand dunes; extensive wind-blown sand deposits - Found mainly in hot deserts - Example: Sahara Desert (Africa), Rub' al Khali (Arabian Peninsula) - Reg (Stony or Rocky Desert) - Surface covered with gravel or pebbles; flat and wind-polished - Sparse vegetation; lacks sand dunes - Example: Gobi Desert (China/Mongolia), Mojave Desert (USA) - Hamada (Barren, Hard Rock Desert) - Consists of exposed bedrock or hard rocky surfaces - Formed due to deflation and erosion removing finer materials - Example: Central Sahara (Africa), Negev Desert (Israel) - Examples: - Thar Desert (India/Pakistan) - Sahara Desert (Africa) - Gobi Desert (China/Mongolia) - Atacama Desert (Chile) - Coastal Landforms - Coastal landforms are shaped by the interaction between the land and the sea, influenced by waves, tides, and currents. These landforms are constantly evolving due to coastal erosion, deposition, and the dynamic nature of the ocean. - Types of Coastal Landforms: - Cliffs - Coastal cliffs are steep rock faces found along coasts, formed through the erosion of softer rocks and the weathering of harder rocks. - They are typically seen where the land meets the sea, particularly along active coasts. - Example: White Cliffs of Dover (England), Cliffs of Moher (Ireland) - Beaches - Beaches are formed by the deposition of sand, pebbles, or cobbles along the shoreline. - They are shaped by the action of waves and tides, which transport and deposit material from the sea. - Example: Waikiki Beach (Hawaii), Copacabana Beach (Brazil) - Sea Arches - Sea arches are formed when waves erode the base of a coastal headland, creating a natural arch-like structure. - The erosion happens along cracks or joints in the rock, often producing spectacular formations. - Example: Arch Rock (USA), London Arch (Australia) - Sea Stacks - Sea stacks are vertical columns of rock that remain standing after the erosion of a sea arch. - These formations are typically isolated and stand out in the water after the arch has collapsed. - Example: Old Man of Hoy (Scotland), Twelve Apostles (Australia) - Spits and Bars - Spits are narrow, elongated sand or gravel formations that project from the shoreline into the water, often formed by longshore drift. - Bars are submerged or partially submerged ridges of sand that form across the mouth of a bay or river, cutting off the flow of water. - Example: Spurn Head (England), Sandy Hook (USA) - Lagoons - Lagoons are shallow bodies of water separated from the sea by a barrier, such as a sandbar, reef, or barrier island. - They are typically calm, sheltered areas where sediments accumulate, forming a unique ecosystem. - Example: Chilika Lake (India), Venice Lagoon (Italy) - Examples: - White Cliffs of Dover (England) - Waikiki Beach (Hawaii) - Arch Rock (USA) - Sandy Hook (USA) - Chilika Lake (India) - Fluvial Landforms (River-based) - Fluvial landforms are created by the processes of erosion, transportation, and deposition by rivers and streams. These landforms are dynamic and constantly change due to the movement of water and sediments. - Types of Fluvial Landforms: - V-shaped Valleys - V-shaped valleys are formed by the erosive action of rivers or streams cutting into the land over long periods of time. - These valleys are characterized by their steep, sloping sides that form a “V” shape due to the downward erosion of the river. - Example: Grand Canyon (USA), River valleys in the Himalayas - Waterfalls - Waterfalls are formed when a river or stream flows over a vertical or near-vertical drop in the landscape. - The difference in rock hardness and the rapid flow of water causes erosion, leading to the formation of a waterfall. - Example: Niagara Falls (Canada/USA), Victoria Falls (Zambia/Zimbabwe) - Meanders - Meanders are winding curves or bends in a river’s course that occur due to erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank of the river. - They form over time as the river seeks a more efficient path through the landscape. - Example: Mississippi River (USA), Ganga River (India) - Oxbow Lakes - Oxbow lakes are formed when a meander of a river is cut off from the main channel, creating a crescent-shaped lake. - These lakes are typically formed during floods when the river breaches the meander neck and redirects its course. - Example: Oxbow Lake in the Nile Delta, Oxbow Lakes in the Yangtze River (China) - Floodplains - Floodplains are flat, low-lying areas adjacent to rivers that are prone to flooding. - They are formed by the deposition of fine sediments (silt, sand, clay) carried by floodwaters, making them highly fertile and good for agriculture. - Example: Indo-Gangetic Plain (India), Nile Floodplain (Egypt) - Alluvial Fans - Alluvial fans are fan-shaped deposits of sediment formed where a river or stream flows from a mountainous region onto a flatter plain or valley floor. - These fans are created when the velocity of the river decreases, causing the sediments to be deposited. - Example: Alluvial Fans in the Mojave Desert (USA), In the foothills of the Himalayas - Deltas - Deltas are formed where a river meets a body of water such as an ocean, sea, or lake, and the flow of water slows down, causing the river to deposit its sediments. - These deposits build up over time, creating a fan or triangular-shaped landform. - Example: Ganges Delta (India/Bangladesh), Nile Delta (Egypt) - Examples: - Grand Canyon (USA) - Niagara Falls (Canada/USA) - Mississippi River (USA) - Oxbow Lakes in the Nile Delta (Egypt) - Indo-Gangetic Plain (India) - Alluvial Fans in Mojave Desert (USA) - Ganges Delta (India/Bangladesh) - Aeolian Landforms (Wind-based) - Aeolian landforms are those created by the action of wind. Wind erosion, transportation, and deposition play a significant role in shaping landscapes, especially in arid and semi-arid regions where vegetation is sparse. - Types of Aeolian Landforms: - Loess Deposits - Loess is a fine, silty sediment deposited by wind. These deposits form extensive, flat, fertile plains in areas with significant wind erosion. - Loess is highly productive for agriculture due to its fine-grained material that retains moisture well. - Example: Loess Plateau in China, Loess deposits in the Midwest (USA) - Sand Dunes (Barchans, Seifs) - Sand dunes are mounds of sand accumulated by the action of wind. Their shape and size depend on the wind's direction, velocity, and the amount of sand available. - Types of Sand Dunes: - Barchans: Crescent-shaped dunes with horns pointing downwind. These dunes form in areas with limited sand supply and unidirectional wind. - Seifs: Long, linear dunes formed in areas with wind blowing from multiple directions, often forming parallel ridges. - Example: Barchans in the Sahara Desert, Seifs in the Kalahari Desert (Africa) - Yardangs - Yardangs are streamlined, wind-sculpted ridges or hills formed by wind erosion in arid regions. They are typically aligned with the prevailing wind direction. - Yardangs are formed by wind carving through rock and sediment, resulting in ridged and elongated landforms. - Example: Yardangs in the Gobi Desert (Mongolia), Yardangs in the Atacama Desert (Chile) - Mushroom Rocks - Mushroom rocks are unique, mushroom-shaped rock formations created by wind erosion. The base of the rock erodes more rapidly than the top, giving them a distinct "mushroom" appearance. - These formations are often found in arid or semi-arid regions where wind erosion is prevalent. - Example: Mushroom Rocks in the Badlands (USA), Mushroom Rocks in the Wadi Rum Desert (Jordan) - Examples: - Loess Plateau in China - Sahara Desert (Africa) - Gobi Desert (Mongolia) - Atacama Desert (Chile) - Badlands (USA) - Wadi Rum Desert (Jordan) - Glacial Landforms - These are landforms created by the action of glaciers, either by erosion or deposition. - These include: - Erosional Landforms: - Cirques (Corries): - Bowl-shaped depressions on mountain sides formed by glacier plucking and abrasion. - U-shaped Valleys: - Glacial troughs with a distinct U-profile formed by glacial erosion replacing V-shaped river valleys. - Aretes: - Sharp ridges formed between two cirques or glacial valleys. - Horns: - Pyramidal peaks formed when several cirques erode a mountain from different sides. - Depositional Landforms: - Moraines: - Accumulations of debris (till) deposited by glaciers. - Types: Lateral, Medial, Terminal, Ground Moraines. - Drumlins: - Streamlined hills composed of glacial till, indicating the direction of glacial movement. - Eskers: - Long, winding ridges of sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams within or beneath glaciers. - Kettles (Kettle Lakes): - Depressions formed by the melting of buried ice blocks in glacial deposits, often filled with water. - Karst Landforms (Limestone regions) - Karst topography develops in regions underlain by soluble rocks, especially limestone, due to chemical weathering and solution processes by slightly acidic water. - These include: - Sinkholes: - Depressions or holes in the ground caused by the collapse of a surface layer. - Formed by dissolution of limestone or collapse of cave roofs. - Dolines: - Larger, bowl-shaped depressions similar to sinkholes. - Can form by solution, collapse, or subsidence of the ground. - Caves (or Caverns): - Underground voids formed by the dissolution of limestone by acidic groundwater. - Often interconnected with passages and chambers. - Stalactites and Stalagmites: - Stalactites hang from cave ceilings (formed by dripping mineral-rich water). - Stalagmites rise from the cave floor (from dripping water accumulating minerals). - When they meet, they form a column or pillar. - Limestone Pavement: - Flat, exposed limestone surface characterized by clints (blocks) and grikes (fissures). - Formed by weathering and chemical erosion over time. - Additional Features: - Poljes: Large, flat-floored depressions with steep sides, common in the Dinaric Alps. - Lapies: Grooved and fluted rock surfaces found on exposed limestone due to dissolution. - Volcanic landforms - Volcanic landforms are diverse geological features shaped by volcanic activity, ranging from small cones and lava flows to large islands and plateaus - Volcanic landforms are closely associated with plate boundaries, hot spots, and rift zones - Some volcanic features (e.g., calderas, flood basalts, mid-ocean ridges) may not form classic cones but are geologically significant - Based on formation location - Extrusive landforms (surface volcanism) - Formed when magma cools and solidifies at the Earth’s crust - Volcanoes (classified by morphology and eruption style) - - Shield volcanoes - Broad, gentle-sloped structures made primarily of basaltic lava - Lava is low-viscosity and highly fluid, enabling wide horizontal spread - Non-explosive to mildly explosive; eruptions resemble lava fountains - Water contact can cause explosive activity - Example: Hawaiian volcanoes (Mauna Loa, Kilauea) - Composite volcanoes (Stratovolcanoes) - Tall, conical volcanoes with layered structure (lava, ash, pyroclastics) - Lava is more viscous [andesitic to rhyolitic], resulting in explosive eruptions - Most common volcano type at subduction zones - Example: Mount Fuji (Japan), Mount St. Helens (USA) - Cinder cone volcanoes - Small, steep-sided cones formed from pyroclastic fragments - Built from ejected lava fragments that solidify in the air and fall around the vent - Short-lived and localized - Often occur around larger volcanoes or shield volcano vents - Lava domes (Volcanic domes) - Formed by slow extrusion of highly viscous, silica-rich lava (rhyolite) - Lava piles up near the vent, forming steep, dome-shaped features - Prone to sudden collapse and explosive pyroclastic flows - Example: Novarupta Dome (Alaska), Mount Unzen (Japan) - Caldera volcanoes - - Formed by extremely violent eruptions followed by collapse of emptied magma chamber - Large circular depressions often filled with water or renewed volcanism - Among the most explosive volcano types - Example: Yellowstone Caldera (USA), Toba Caldera (Indonesia) - Flood basalt provinces (also called Plateau Basalts) - - Massive, widespread lava outpourings of highly fluid basaltic lava - Repeated eruptions form flat, layered plateaus - Lava flows can cover thousands of square kilometers - Example: Deccan Traps (India), Columbia River Basalt Group (USA) - Mid-ocean ridge volcanoes - - Form at divergent plate boundaries along mid-ocean ridges - Basaltic eruptions due to decompression melting - Constant submarine eruptions, forming new oceanic crust - Over 70,000 km long ridge system across ocean floors - Example: Mid-Atlantic Ridge - Other extrusive forms - Lava Plateaus - - Extensive, flat-topped regions formed by repeated lava flows - Example: Deccan Plateau, Columbia Plateau - Intrusive landforms (subsurface volcanism) - - - Formed when magma cools and solidifies within the Earth’s crust - These bodies become exposed over time due to erosion of overlying rocks - These include: - Batholiths - Very large, dome-shaped intrusive igneous bodies formed deep in the crust - Granitic in composition and may span hundreds of kilometers - Represent cooled magma chambers - Exposed after denudation [process in which moving water, ice, wind, etc eroding the earth's surface] removes overlying rock layers - Laccoliths - Dome-shaped masses with a flat base, connected to magma source by conduit - Similar to surface volcanic domes but remain underground - Example: Granite domes in Karnataka plateau - Lopoliths - Saucer-shaped intrusions, concave upward - Formed when magma spreads horizontally after partial ascent - Heavier in center due to subsidence of overlying rocks - Phacoliths - Lens-shaped or wavy intrusive bodies found along fold structures (anticlines/synclines) - Typically aligned with the folding of surrounding rock layers - Sills - Horizontal sheet-like intrusions along bedding planes - Formed by magma pushing between rock layers - Thin ones are called sheets; thicker ones are sills - Dykes - Vertical or steeply inclined wall-like structures - Formed when magma forces through cracks perpendicular to rock layers - Commonly observed in Maharashtra’s Deccan region - Act as feeders for flood basalt eruptions - Oceanic Landforms (Submarine) - These landforms lie beneath the ocean surface and are formed by tectonic, volcanic, and sedimentary processes. - These include: - Continental Shelf - The submerged, gently sloping extension of the continent under shallow sea. - Rich in marine life and resources like oil and gas. - Width varies greatly—wide along Atlantic coasts, narrow along Pacific coasts. - Example: Siberian Shelf (widest), eastern coast of India. - Continental Slope - Steep slope between the outer edge of the continental shelf and the deep ocean floor. - Marks the true edge of the continental mass. - Subject to submarine landslides and turbidity currents. - Abyssal Plain - Deep, flat, and extensive plains on the ocean floor at depths of 3,000 to 6,000 meters. - Formed by the accumulation of fine sediments and volcanic material. - Among the flattest and smoothest regions on Earth. - Example: Sohm Plain (Atlantic Ocean) - Mid-Ocean Ridge - Underwater mountain range formed by divergent tectonic plates at spreading centers. - Associated with volcanic activity and hydrothermal vents. - Example: Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East Pacific Rise. - Ocean Trenches - Long, narrow, and deepest depressions on the ocean floor, formed by subduction zones. - Sites of intense geological activity (earthquakes, tsunamis). - Example: Mariana Trench (deepest), Java Trench. - Seamounts and Guyots - Seamounts: Underwater volcanic mountains that do not reach the surface. - Example: Davidson Seamount (Pacific Ocean). - Guyots: Seamounts that were once above sea level but became flat-topped due to erosion and later submerged. - Example: Horizon Guyot. - Classification of landforms - Based on Origin (Genetic Classification) 1. Endogenic Landforms (formed by internal forces) - Result from tectonic and volcanic activity - Examples: - Mountains (Fold, Block, Volcanic) - Plateaus - Rift Valleys - Domes 2. Exogenic Landforms (formed by external forces) - Result from weathering, erosion, transportation, and deposition by agents like rivers, wind, glaciers, and waves - Examples: - Riverine features: valleys, meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains, deltas - Aeolian features: sand dunes, loess - Glacial features: cirques, moraines, U-shaped valleys - Coastal features: cliffs, stacks, arches, beaches - Karst features: sinkholes, stalactites, stalagmites - Based on Size (Morphological or Scale Classification) 1. Major Landforms - Large-scale features formed primarily by endogenic processes - Examples: - Mountains - Plateaus - Plains 2. Minor Landforms - Medium-scale surface features formed by erosion and deposition - Examples: - Hills - Escarpments - Terraces - Cliffs - Valleys 3. Micro Landforms - Small-scale features, often local in extent, formed by both endogenic and exogenic processes - Examples: - Ripple marks - Potholes - Sand dunes - Yardangs - Sinkholes - Geomorphic agents and resulting landforms - Some exogenic agents - Running water - Importance and components - In humid regions, which receive heavy rainfall running water is considered the most important of the geomorphic agents in bringing about the degradation of the land surface - There are two components of running water - One is overland flow on general land surface as a sheet - Another is linear flow as streams and rivers in valleys - Erosional processes - Most of the erosional landforms made by running water are associated with vigorous [strong / healthy] and youthful rivers flowing over steep [rising or falling sharply] gradients [a slope] - With time, stream [small, narrow river] channels [waterway] over steep gradients turn gentler [lenient] due to continued erosion, and as a consequence [result], lose their velocity, facilitating [make easier] active deposition - There may be depositional forms associated with streams flowing over steep slopes - But these phenomena will be on a small scale compared to those associated with rivers flowing over medium to gentle slopes - The gentler the river channels in gradient or slope, the greater is the deposition - When the stream beds turn gentler due to continued erosion, downward cutting becomes less dominant and lateral [sideways] erosion of banks increases and as a consequence the hills and valleys are reduced to plains - Is complete reduction of relief of a high land mass possible? - Overland flow causes sheet erosion - Depending upon irregularities of the land surface, the overland flow may concentrate into narrow to wide paths - Because of the sheer friction of the column of flowing water, minor or major quantities of materials from the surface of the land are removed in the direction of flow and gradually small and narrow rills will form - These rills will gradually develop into long and wide gullies; the gullies [pass] will further deepen, widen, lengthen and unite to give rise to a network of valleys - In the early stages, down-cutting dominates during which irregularities such as waterfalls and cascades [small waterfalls in stages] will be removed - In the middle stages, streams cut their beds slower, and lateral erosion of valley sides becomes severe - Gradually, the valley sides are reduced to lower and lower slopes - The divides between drainage basins are likewise lowered until they are almost completely flattened leaving finally, a lowland of faint relief with some low resistant remnants [remains] called monadnocks standing out here and there - This type of plain forming as a result of stream erosion is called a peneplain (an almost plain) - Stages of landscape development - Overview - The characteristics of each of the stages of landscapes developing in running water regimes may be summarised as follows: - Youth - Streams are few during this stage with poor integration and flow over original slopes showing shallow V-shaped valleys with no floodplains or with very narrow floodplains along trunk streams - Streams divides are broad and flat with marshes, swamp and lakes - Meanders [a winding curve or bend of river or road / zig-zag] if present develop over these broad upland surfaces - These meanders may eventually entrench themselves into the uplands - Waterfalls and rapids may exist where local hard rock bodies are exposed - Mature - During this stage streams are plenty with good integration - The valleys are still V-shaped but deep; trunk [major] streams are broad enough to have wider floodplains within which streams may flow in meanders confined within the valley - The flat and broad inter stream areas and swamps and marshes of youth disappear and the stream divides turn sharp - Waterfalls and rapids disappear - Old - Smaller tributaries during old age are few with gentle gradients - Streams meander freely over vast floodplains showing natural levees, oxbow lakes, etc. - Divides are broad and flat with lakes, swamps and marshes - Most of the landscape is at or slightly above sea level - Erosional landforms - Valleys - - Valleys start as small and narrow rills; the rills will gradually develop into long and wide gullies; the gullies will further deepen, widen and lengthen to give rise to valleys - Depending upon dimensions and shape, many types of valleys: - - V-shaped valley - U-shaped valley - A gorge is a deep valley with very steep to straight sides (Figure 7.1). A gorge is almost equal in width at its top as well as its bottom - A canyon is characterised by steep steplike side slopes (Figure 7.2) and may be as deep as a gorge. A canyon is wider at its top than at its bottom. - In fact, a canyon is a variant of gorge - Valley types depend upon the type and structure of rocks in which they form - For example, canyons commonly form in horizontal bedded sedimentary rocks and gorges form in hard rocks - - Potholes and plunge pools - - Over the rocky beds of hill-streams more or less circular depressions called potholes form because of stream erosion aided by the abrasion of rock fragments - Once a small and shallow depression forms, pebbles and boulders get collected in those depressions and get rotated by flowing water and consequently the depressions grow in dimensions - A series of such depressions eventually join and the stream valley gets deepened - At the foot of waterfalls also, large potholes, quite deep and wide, form because of the sheer impact of water and rotation of boulders - Such large and deep holes at the base of waterfalls are called plunge pools - Incised or entrenched meanders - - - In streams that flow rapidly over steep gradients, normally erosion is concentrated on the bottom of the stream channel - Also, in the case of steep gradient streams, lateral erosion on the sides of the valleys is not much when compared to the streams flowing on low and gentle slopes - Because of active lateral erosion, streams flowing over gentle slopes, develop sinuous [having many curves and turns] or meandering courses - It is common to find meandering courses over floodplains and delta plains where stream gradients are very gentle - But very deep and wide meanders can also be found cut in hard rocks - Such meanders are called incised or entrenched meanders (Figure 7.2) - River terraces - - River terraces are surfaces marking old valley floor or floodplain levels - They may be bedrock surfaces without any alluvial cover or alluvial terraces consisting of stream deposits - River terraces are basically products of erosion as they result due to vertical erosion by the stream into its own depositional floodplain - There can be a number of such terraces at different heights indicating former river bed levels - The river terraces may occur at the same elevation on either side of the rivers in which case they are called paired terraces - Depositional landforms - Alluvial fans - - - Alluvial fans (Figure 7.4) are formed when streams flowing from higher levels break into foot slope plains of low gradient - Normally very coarse load is carried by streams flowing over mountain slopes - This load becomes too heavy for the streams to be carried over gentler gradients and gets dumped and spread as a broad low to high cone shaped deposit called alluvial fan - Usually, the streams which flow over fans are not confined to their original channels for long and shift their position across the fan forming many channels called distributaries - Alluvial fans in humid areas show normally low cones with gentle slope from head to toe and they appear as high cones with steep slope in arid and semi-arid climates - Deltas - - - Deltas are like alluvial fans but develop at a different location - The load carried by the rivers is dumped and spread into the sea - If this load is not carried away far into the sea or distributed along the coast, it spreads and accumulates as a low cone - Unlike in alluvial fans, the deposits making up deltas are very well sorted with clear stratification [the arrangement or classification of something into different groups] - The coarsest materials settle out first and the finer fractions like silts and clays are carried out into the sea - As the delta grows, the river distributaries continue to increase in length (Figure 7.5) and delta continues to build up into the sea - Types of delta - - Floodplains, natural levees and point bars - - - Floodplains - Deposition develops a floodplain just as erosion makes valleys - Floodplain is a major landform of river deposition - Large sized materials are deposited first when stream channel breaks into a gentle slope - Thus, normally, fine sized materials like sand, silt and clay are carried by relatively slow moving waters in gentler channels usually found in the plains and deposited over the bed and when the waters spill over the banks during flooding above the bed - A river bed made of river deposits is the active floodplain - The floodplain above the bank is inactive floodplain - Inactive floodplain above the banks basically contain two types of deposits — Flood deposits - Channel deposits - In plains, channels shift laterally and change their courses occasionally leaving cut-off courses which get filled up gradually [slowly] - Such areas over flood plains built up by abandoned or cut-off channels contain coarse deposits - The flood deposits of spilled waters carry relatively finer materials like silt and clay - The flood plains in a delta are called delta plains - Natural levees and point bars (Figure 7.6) are some of the important landforms found associated with floodplains - Natural levees - Natural levees are found along the banks of large rivers - They are low, linear and parallel ridges of coarse deposits along the banks of rivers, quite often cut into individual mounds - Point bars - Point bars are also known as meander bars - They are found on the concave side of meanders of large rivers and are sediments deposited in a linear fashion by flowing waters along the bank - They are almost uniform in profile and in width and contain mixed sizes of sediments - In what way do natural levees differ from point bars? -
Feature Natural Levees Point Bars
Location Along the riverbanks on the floodplain On the inner side of meander bends
Formation Process Formed by deposition during floods when river overflows and deposits coarser sediments near banks Formed by slow-flowing water depositing sediments on the inside curve of a river bend
Composition Mainly silt and sand Sand, gravel, and fine sediments
Function Act as natural embankments, reducing minor flooding Temporary depositional features that change with river flow
Shape Broad and gently sloping away from the river Crescent-shaped or scroll-like
- Meanders - - - In large flood and delta plains, rivers rarely flow in straight courses - Loop-like channel patterns called meanders develop over flood and delta plains (Figure 7.7) - Meander is not a landform but is only a type of channel pattern, this is because of: - Propensity [tendency] of water flowing over very gentle gradients to work laterally on the banks - Unconsolidated nature of alluvial deposits making up the banks with many irregularities which can be used by water exerting pressure laterally - Coriolis force acting on the fluid water deflecting it like it deflects the wind - When the gradient of the channel becomes extremely low, water flows leisurely [relaxed] and starts working laterally - Slight irregularities along the banks slowly get transformed into a small curvature in the banks; the curvature deepens due to deposition on the inside of the curve and erosion along the bank on the outside - If there is no deposition and no erosion or undercutting, the tendency to meander is reduced - Normally, in meanders of large rivers, there is active deposition along the concave bank and undercutting along the convex bank - The concave bank is known as cut-off bank which shows up as a steep scarp and the convex bank presents a long, gentle profile (Figure 7.8) - As meanders grow into deep loops, the same may get cut-off due to erosion at the inflection points and are left as ox-bow lakes - Groundwater - - - Overview - Here the interest is not on groundwater as a resource - Our focus is on the work of groundwater in the erosion of landmasses and evolution of landforms - The surface water percolates [filter gradually through a porous surface] well when the rocks are permeable, thinly bedded and highly jointed and cracked - After vertically going down to some depth, the water under the ground flows horizontally through the bedding planes, joints or through the materials themselves - It is this downward and horizontal movement of water which causes the rocks to erode - Physical or mechanical removal of materials by moving groundwater is insignificant in developing landforms - That is why, the results of the work of groundwater cannot be seen in all types of rocks - But in rocks like limestones or dolomites rich in calcium carbonate, the surface water as well as groundwater through the chemical process of solution and precipitation deposition develop varieties of landforms - These two processes of solution and precipitation are active in limestones or dolomites occurring either exclusively or interbedded with other rocks - Any limestone or dolomitic region showing typical landforms produced by the action of groundwater through the processes of solution and deposition is called Karst topography after the typical topography developed in limestone rocks of Karst region in the Balkans adjacent to Adriatic sea - The karst topography is also characterised by erosional and depositional landforms - Erosional landforms - Pools, sinkholes, lapies and limestone pavements - Small to medium sized round to sub-rounded shallow depressions called swallow holes form on the surface of limestones through solution - Sinkholes are very common in limestone/karst areas - A sinkhole is an opening more or less circular at the top and funnel-shaped towards the bottom with sizes varying in area from a few sq. m to a hectare and with depth from a less than half a metre to thirty metres or more - Some of these form solely through solution action (solution sinks) and others might start as solution forms first and if the bottom of a sinkhole forms the roof of a void or cave underground, it might collapse leaving a large hole opening into a cave or a void below (collapse sinks) - Quite often, sinkholes are covered up with soil mantle and appear as shallow water pools - Anybody stepping over such pools would go down like it happens in quicksands in deserts - The term doline is sometimes used to refer the collapse sinks - Solution sinks are more common than collapse sinks - Quite often the surface runoff simply goes down swallow and sink holes and flow as underground streams and re-emerge at a distance downstream through a cave opening - When sink holes and dolines join together because of slumping of materials along their margins or due to roof collapse of caves, long, narrow to wide trenches called valley sinks or Uvalas form - Gradually, most of the surface of the limestone is eaten away by these pits and trenches, leaving it extremely irregular with a maze of points, grooves and ridges or lapies - Especially, these ridges or lapies form due to differential solution activity along parallel to sub-parallel joints - The lapie field may eventually turn into somewhat smooth limestone pavements - Caves - In areas where there are alternating beds of rocks (shales, sandstones, quartzites) with limestones or dolomites in between or in areas where limestones are dense, massive and occurring as thick beds, cave formation is prominent - Water percolates [filter gradually through a porous surface] down either through the materials or through cracks and joints and moves horizontally along bedding planes - It is along these bedding planes that the limestone dissolves and long and narrow to wide gaps called caves result - There can be a maze of caves at different elevations depending upon the limestone beds and intervening rocks - Caves normally have an opening through which cave streams are discharged - Caves having openings at both the ends are called tunnels - Depositional landforms - Overview - Many depositional forms develop within the limestone caves - The chief chemical in limestone is calcium carbonate which is easily soluble in carbonated water (carbon dioxide absorbed rainwater) - This calcium carbonate is deposited when the water carrying it in solution evaporates or loses its carbon dioxide as it trickles over rough rock surfaces - Stalactites, stalagmites and pillars - - Stalactites hang as icicles of different diameters - Normally they are broad at their bases and taper towards the free ends showing up in a variety of forms - Stalagmites rise up from the floor of the caves - In fact, stalagmites form due to dripping water from the surface or through the thin pipe, of the stalactite, immediately below it (Figure 7.11) - Stalagmites may take the shape of a column, a disc, with either a smooth, rounded bulging end or a miniature crater like depression - The stalagmite and stalactites eventually fuse to give rise to columns and pillars of different diameters - Glaciers - - Overview - Masses of ice moving as sheets over the land (continental glacier or piedmont glacier if a vast sheet of ice is spread over the plains at the foot of mountains) or as linear flows down the slopes of mountains in broad trough-like valleys (mountain and valley glaciers) are called glaciers (Figure 7.12) - The movement of glaciers is slow unlike water flow - The movement could be a few centimetres to a few metres a day or even less or more - Glaciers move basically because of the force of gravity - We have many glaciers in our country moving down the slopes and valleys in Himalayas - Higher reaches of Uttaranchal, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir, are places to see some of them - Do you know where one can see river Bhagirathi is basically fed by meltwaters from under the snout [the projecting nose or mouth of an animal] (Gaumukh) of the Gangotri glacier - In fact, Alkapuri glacier feeds waters to Alakananda river - Rivers Alkananda and Bhagirathi join to make river Ganga near Deoprayag - Erosion by glaciers is tremendous [enormous / colossal / very great] because of friction caused by sheer weight of the ice - The material plucked from the land by glaciers (usually large-sized angular blocks and fragments) get dragged along the floors or sides of the valleys and cause great damage through abrasion and plucking - Glaciers can cause significant damage to even unweathered rocks and can reduce high mountains into low hills and plains - As glaciers continue to move, debris gets removed, divides get lowered and eventually the slope is reduced to such an extent that glaciers will stop moving leaving only a mass of low hills and vast outwash plains along with other depositional features - Figures 7.13 and 7.14 show various glacial erosional and depositional forms described in the text - Erosional landforms - - - Cirque - Cirques are the most common of landforms in glaciated mountains - The cirques quite often are found at the heads of glacial valleys - The accumulated ice cuts these cirques while moving down the mountain tops - They are deep, long and wide troughs or basins with very steep concave to vertically dropping high walls at its head as well as sides - A lake of water can be seen quite often within the cirques after the glacier disappears - Such lakes are called cirque or tarn lakes - There can be two or more cirques one leading into another down below in a stepped sequence - Horns and serrated ridges - Horns form through head ward erosion of the cirque walls - If three or more radiating glaciers cut headward until their cirques meet, high, sharp pointed and steep sided peaks called horns form - The divides between cirque side walls or head walls get narrow because of progressive erosion and turn into serrated or saw-toothed ridges sometimes referred to as arêtes with very sharp crest and a zig-zag outline - The highest peak in the Alps, Matterhorn and the highest peak in the Himalayas, Everest are in fact horns formed through headward erosion of radiating cirques - Glacial valleys/troughs - Glaciated valleys are trough-like and U shaped with broad floors and relatively smooth, and steep sides - The valleys may contain littered debris or debris shaped as moraines with swampy appearance - There may be lakes gouged [scoop out / excavate] out of rocky floor or formed by debris within the valleys - There can be hanging valleys at an elevation on one or both sides of the main glacial valley - A hanging valley is a tributary valley whose floor is located at a higher elevation than the floor of the main, larger valley - The faces of divides or spurs of such hanging valleys opening into main glacial valleys are quite often truncated [shorten in duration or extend] to give them an appearance like triangular facets [one side of many sided] - Very deep glacial troughs [long, narrow, open body or container for animals to drink] filled with sea water and making up shorelines (in high latitudes) are called fjords/fiords - What are the basic differences between glacial valleys and river valleys? -
Feature Glacial Valley River Valley
Shape U-shaped V-shaped
Formation Agent Glaciers (moving ice) Rivers (flowing water)
Erosion Type Plucking and abrasion by ice Downcutting by water flow
Valley Sides Steep and straight Steep but more angular
Location Typically in high mountains and polar areas Found in most terrains
Examples Valleys in the Alps, Himalayas (e.g., Pindari Glacier) Ganga Valley, Indus Valley
- Depositional landforms - - - Overview - The unassorted [not having been grouped or categorized] coarse [rough or harsh in texture / consisting of large grains] and fine [thin / small/ good quality] debris [waste / scattered pieces of rubbish or remains] dropped by the melting glaciers is called glacial till - Most of the rock fragments in till are angular to sub-angular in form - Streams form by melting ice at the bottom, sides or lower ends of glaciers - Some amount of rock debris small enough to be carried by such melt-water streams is washed down and deposited - Such glacio-fluvial deposits are called outwash deposits - Unlike till deposits, the outwash deposits are roughly stratified [formed or arranged into strata or layers] and assorted [of various sorts put together] - The rock fragments in outwash deposits are somewhat rounded at their edges - Figure 7.14 shows a few depositional landforms commonly found in glaciated areas - Moraines - They are long ridges of deposits of glacial till - Terminal moraines are long ridges of debris deposited at the end (toe) of the glaciers - Lateral moraines form along the sides parallel to the glacial valleys - The lateral moraines may join a terminal moraine forming a horse-shoe shaped ridge (Fig. 7.13) - There can be many lateral moraines on either side in a glacial valley - These moraines partly or fully owe their origin to glacio-fluvial waters pushing up materials to the sides of glaciers - Many valley glaciers retreating rapidly leave an irregular sheet of till over their valley floors - Such deposits varying greatly in thickness and in surface topography are called ground moraines - The moraine in the centre of the glacial valley flanked by lateral moraines is called medial moraine - They are imperfectly formed as compared to lateral moraines - Sometimes medial moraines are indistinguishable from ground moraines - Eskers - When glaciers melt in summer, the water flows on the surface of the ice or seeps down along the margins or even moves through holes in the ice - These waters accumulate beneath the glacier and flow like streams in a channel beneath the ice - Such streams flow over the ground (not in a valley cut in the ground) with ice forming its banks - Very coarse materials like boulders and blocks along with some minor fractions of rock debris carried into this stream settle in the valley of ice beneath the glacier and after the ice melts can be found as a sinuous [having many curves and turns] ridge called esker - Outwash plains - The plains at the foot of the glacial mountains or beyond the limits of continental ice sheets are covered with glacio-fluvial deposits in the form of broad flat alluvial fans which may join to form outwash plains of gravel, silt, sand and clay - Distinguish between river alluvial plains and glacial outwash plains - Drumlins - Drumlins are smooth oval shaped ridge-like features composed mainly of glacial till with some masses of gravel and sand - The long axes of drumlins are parallel to the direction of ice movement - They may measure up to 1 km in length and 30 m or so in height - One end of the drumlins facing the glacier called the stoss end is blunter and steeper than the other end called tail - The drumlins form due to dumping of rock debris beneath heavily loaded ice through fissures in the glacier - The stoss end gets blunted due to pushing by moving ice - Drumlins give an indication of direction of glacier movement - What is the difference between till and alluvium? -
Feature Till Alluvium
Origin Deposited directly by glaciers Deposited by rivers or running water
Sorting Unsorted and unstratified (contains mixed sizes of particles) Well-sorted and stratified (layered by particle size)
Material Composition Clay, sand, gravel, boulders mixed randomly Sand, silt, clay, and fine sediments
Depositional Environment Glacial (continental or alpine glaciers) Fluvial (rivers, floodplains, deltas)
Appearance Heterogeneous and rough Homogeneous and layered
- Waves and currents - Overview - Coastal processes are the most dynamic and hence most destructive - So, don’t you think it is important to know about the coastal processes and forms? - Some of the changes along the coasts take place very fast - At one place, there can be erosion in one season and deposition in another - Most of the changes along the coasts are accomplished by waves - When waves break, the water is thrown with great force onto the shore, and simultaneously, there is a great churning [move or cause to move about vigorously] of sediments on the sea bottom - Constant impact of breaking waves drastically affects the coasts - Storm waves and tsunami waves can cause far-reaching changes in a short period of time than normal breaking waves - As wave environment changes, the intensity of the force of breaking waves changes - Do you know about the generating forces behind waves and currents? If not, refer to the chapter on movements in ocean waters - Other than the action of waves, the coastal landforms depend upon: - The configuration of land and sea floor - Whether the coast is advancing (emerging) seaward or retreating (submerging) landward - Assuming sea level to be constant, two types of coasts are considered to explain the concept of evolution of coastal landforms: - High, rocky coasts (submerged coasts) - Low, smooth and gently sloping sedimentary coasts - - High rocky coasts - Along the high rocky coasts, the rivers appear to have been drowned with highly irregular coastline - The coastline appears highly indented [move further from margin] with extension of water into the land where glacial valleys (fjords) are present - The hill sides drop off sharply into the water - Shores do not show any depositional landforms initially - Erosion features dominate - Along high rocky coasts, waves break with great force against the land shaping the hill sides into cliffs - With constant pounding by waves, the cliffs recede leaving a wave-cut platform in front of the sea cliff - Waves gradually minimise the irregularities along the shore - The materials which fall off, and removed from the sea cliffs, gradually break into smaller fragments and roll to roundness, will get deposited in the offshore - After a considerable period of cliff development and retreat when coastline turns somewhat smooth, with the addition of some more material to this deposit in the offshore, a wave-built terrace would develop in front of wave-cut terrace - As the erosion along the coast takes place a good supply material becomes available to longshore currents and waves to deposit them as beaches along the shore and as bars (long ridges of sand and/or shingle parallel to the coast) in the nearshore zone - Bars are submerged features and when bars show up above water, they are called barrier bars - Barrier bar which get keyed up to the headland of a bay is called a spit - When barrier bars and spits form at the mouth of a bay and block it, a lagoon forms - The lagoons would gradually get filled up by sediments from the land giving rise to a coastal plain - Low sedimentary coasts - Along low sedimentary coasts the rivers appear to extend their length by building coastal plains and deltas - The coastline appears smooth with occasional incursions of water in the form of lagoons and tidal creeks - The land slopes gently into the water - Marshes and swamps may abound along the coasts - Depositional features dominate - When waves break over a gently sloping sedimentary coast, the bottom sediments get churned and move readily building bars, barrier bars, spits and lagoons - Lagoons would eventually turn into a swamp which would subsequently turn into a coastal plain - The maintenance of these depositional features depends upon the steady supply of materials - Storm and tsunami waves cause drastic changes irrespective of supply of sediments - Large rivers which bring lots of sediments build deltas along low sedimentary coasts - The west coast of our country is a high rocky retreating coast - Erosional forms dominate in the west coast - The east coast of India is a low sedimentary coast - Depositional forms dominate in the east coast - What are the various differences between a high rocky coast and a low sedimentary coast in terms of processes and landforms? -
Feature High Rocky Coast Low Sedimentary Coast
Elevation Steep, elevated cliffs and headlands Low-lying, flat terrain near sea level
Material Composition Hard rocks like granite, basalt Loose sediments like sand, silt, clay
Dominant Process Marine erosion (abrasion, hydraulic action) Marine deposition (along with minor erosion)
Landforms Cliffs, wave-cut platforms, sea caves, arches, stacks Beaches, spits, bars, lagoons, dunes
Stability More stable and resistant to rapid change Highly dynamic, changes quickly due to deposition and erosion
Examples Western coasts of India (Konkan coast), British Isles Eastern coasts of India (Coromandel coast), Nile Delta
- Erosional landforms - - Cliffs, terraces, caves and stacks - Wave-cut cliffs and terraces are two forms usually found where erosion is the dominant shore process - Almost all sea cliffs are steep and may range from a few m to 30 m or even more - At the foot of such cliffs there may be a flat or gently sloping platform covered by rock debris derived from the sea cliff behind - Such platforms occurring at elevations above the average height of waves is called a wave-cut terrace - The lashing of waves against the base of the cliff and the rock debris that gets smashed against the cliff along with lashing waves create hollows and these hollows get widened and deepened to form sea caves - The roofs of caves collapse and the sea cliffs recede further inland - Retreat of the cliff may leave some remnants of rock standing isolated as small islands just off the shore - Such resistant masses of rock, originally parts of a cliff or hill are called sea stacks - Like all other features, sea stacks are also temporary and eventually coastal hills and cliffs will disappear because of wave erosion giving rise to narrow coastal plains, and with onrush of deposits from over the land behind may get covered up by alluvium or may get covered up by shingle or sand to form a wide beach - Depositional landforms - - Beaches and dunes - Beaches are characteristic of shorelines that are dominated by deposition, but may occur as patches along even the rugged [having broken, rocky or uneven surface] shores [the land along the edge of a water body] - Most of the sediment making up the beaches comes from land carried by the streams and rivers or from wave erosion - Beaches are temporary features - The sandy beach which appears so permanent may be reduced to a very narrow strip of coarse pebbles in some other season - Most of the beaches are made up of sand sized materials - Beaches called shingle beaches contain excessively small pebbles and even cobbles - Just behind the beach, the sands lifted and winnowed [blow] from over the beach surfaces will be deposited as sand dunes - Sand dunes forming long ridges parallel to the coastline are very common along low sedimentary coasts - Bars, barriers and spits - - A ridge of sand and shingle formed in the sea in the off-shore zone (from the position of low tide waterline to seaward) lying approximately parallel to the coast is called an off-shore bar - An off-shore bar which is exposed due to further addition of sand is termed a barrier bar - The off-shore bars and barriers commonly form across the mouth of a river or at the entrance of a bay - Sometimes such barrier bars get keyed up to one end of the bay when they are called spits (Figure 7.15) - Spits may also develop attached to headlands/hills - The barriers, bars and spits at the mouth of the bay gradually extend leaving only a small opening of the bay into the sea and the bay will eventually develop into a lagoon - The lagoons get filled up gradually by sediment coming from the land or from the beach itself (aided by wind) and a broad and wide coastal plain may develop replacing a lagoon - Do you know, the coastal off-shore bars offer the first buffer or defence against storm or tsunami by absorbing most of their destructive force - Then come the barriers, beaches, beach dunes and mangroves, if any, to absorb the destructive force of storm and tsunami waves - So, if we do anything which disturbs the ‘sediment budget’ and the mangroves along the coast, these coastal forms will get eroded away leaving human habitations to bear first strike of storm and tsunami waves - Winds - Overview - Wind is one of the two dominant agents in hot deserts - The desert floors get heated up too much and too quickly because of being dry and barren - The heated floors heat up the air directly above them and result in upward movements in the hot lighter air with turbulence [violent or unsteady movement of air, water or other liquid], and any obstructions in its path sets up eddies, whirlwinds, updrafts and downdrafts - Winds also move along the desert floors with great speed and the obstructions in their path create turbulence - Of course, there are storm winds which are very destructive - Winds cause deflation, abrasion and impact - Deflation includes lifting and removal of dust and smaller particles from the surface of rocks - In the transportation process sand and silt act as effective tools to abrade the land surface - The impact is simply sheer force of momentum which occurs when sand is blown into or against a rock surface - It is similar to sandblasting operation - The wind action creates a number of interesting erosional and depositional features in the deserts - In fact, many features of deserts owe their formation to mass wasting and running water as sheet floods - Though rain is scarce in deserts, it comes down torrentially in a short period of time - The desert rocks devoid [lacking] of vegetation, exposed to mechanical and chemical weathering processes due to drastic [extreme / serious / far-reaching] diurnal [of or during the day / daily / everyday] temperature changes, decay faster and the torrential [heavy / relentless / violent] rains help in removing the weathered materials easily - That means, the weathered debris in deserts is moved by not only wind but also by rain/sheet wash - The wind moves fine materials and general mass erosion is accomplished mainly through sheet floods or sheet wash - Stream channels in desert areas are broad, smooth and indefinite and flow for a brief time after rains - Erosional landforms - - Pediments and pediplains - Landscape evolution in deserts is primarily concerned with the formation and extension of pediments - Gently inclined rocky floors close to the mountains at their foot with or without a thin cover of debris, are called pediments - Such rocky floors form through the erosion of mountain front through a combination of lateral erosion by streams and sheet flooding - Erosion starts along the steep margins of the landmass or the steep sides of the tectonically controlled steep incision features over the landmass - Once, pediments are formed with a steep wash slope followed by cliff or free face above it, the steep wash slope and free face retreat backwards - This method of erosion is termed as parallel retreat of slopes through backwasting - So, through parallel retreat of slopes, the pediments extend backwards at the expense of mountain front, and gradually, the mountain gets reduced leaving an inselberg [an isolated hill or mountain rising abruptly from a plain] which is a remnant of the mountain - That’s how the high relief in desert areas is reduced to low featureless plains called pediplains - Playas - Plains are by far the most prominent landforms in the deserts - In basins with mountains and hills around and along, the drainage is towards the centre of the basin and due to gradual deposition of sediment from basin margins, a nearly level plain forms at the centre of the basin - In times of sufficient water, this plain is covered up by a shallow water body - Such types of shallow lakes are called as playas where water is retained only for short duration due to evaporation and quite often the playas contain good deposition of salts - The playa plain covered up by salts is called alkali flats - Deflation hollows and caves - Weathered mantle from over the rocks or bare soil, gets blown out by persistent movement of wind currents in one direction - This process may create shallow depressions called deflation hollows - Deflation also creates numerous small pits or cavities over rock surfaces - The rock faces suffer impact and abrasion of wind-borne sand and first shallow depressions called blow outs are created, and some of the blow outs become deeper and wider fit to be called caves -
