Capital: Pretoria - South Sudan - Capital: Juba - Sudan - Capital: Khartoum - Tanzania - Capital: Dodoma - Togo - Capital: Lomé - Tunisia - Capital: Tunis - Uganda - Capital: Kampala - Zambia - Capital: Lusaka - Zimbabwe - Capital: Harare - Physiographic Divisions - Africa’s landscape is divided into eight regions: 1. Sahara: - - Description: - Largest hot desert in the world. - Location: - Northern Africa. - Climate: - Arid, extreme temperatures. - Features: - Sand dunes, rocky plateaus (hamadas), gravel plains (regs). - Countries: - Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Mauritania, Sudan, etc. 2. Sahel: - - Description: - Semi-arid zone south of the Sahara; transition zone. - Climate: - Hot, with seasonal rainfall. - Vegetation: - Grasslands, sparse shrubs. - Challenges: - Desertification, overgrazing. - Countries: - Mali, Niger, Chad, Sudan, Burkina Faso, etc. 3. Ethiopian Highlands: - - Description: - Rugged mountainous region; known as the “Roof of Africa”. - Location: - Mainly in Ethiopia and Eritrea. - Climate: - Cooler, highland type. - Features: - Volcanic mountains, plateaus. - Significance: - Source of the Blue Nile River. 4. Savanna: - - Description: - Grassland region with scattered trees. - Climate: - Tropical wet and dry (Aw in Köppen). - Vegetation: - Grasses, acacia trees. - Wildlife: - Lions, elephants, zebras, etc. - Countries: - Kenya, Tanzania, Nigeria, etc. 5. Swahili Coast: - - Description: - Narrow coastal strip along the eastern shore. - Location: - Along the Indian Ocean (Kenya to Mozambique). - Climate: - Tropical, humid. - Features: - Coral reefs, beaches, islands (e.g., Zanzibar). - Significance: - Historic trade region (Arab-African maritime links). 6. Rainforest: - - Description: - Dense tropical rainforest belt. - Location: - Central Africa (especially Congo Basin). - Climate: - Equatorial, hot and humid (Af in Köppen). - Vegetation: - Thick evergreen forests. - Significance: - 2nd largest rainforest after Amazon. 7. African Great Lakes: - - Description: - Series of large freshwater lakes in East Africa. - Notable Lakes: - Victoria, Tanganyika, Malawi. - Features: - Rift Valley lakes, deep basins. - Biodiversity: - High fish diversity (e.g., cichlids). - Importance: - Water resource, fishing, agriculture. 8. Southern Africa: - - Description: - Varied landscape — plateaus, deserts (Kalahari, Namib), and highlands. - Countries: - South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, etc. - Climate: - Ranges from Mediterranean (SW tip) to desert. - Features: - Drakensberg Mountains, Okavango Delta. - Formation: - Ancient Precambrian cratons form stable plateaus and basins, while Cenozoic rifting created the East African Rift and volcanic highlands. - Major Physical Features - Mountain Ranges - Atlas Mountains (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia): - - Description: - Stretches ~2,500 km, peaks at 4,167 m (Toubkal). - Formation: - Collision of African and Eurasian plates during Cenozoic orogeny. - Significance: - Influences Mediterranean climate, supports agriculture. - Ethiopian Highlands (Ethiopia): - - Description: - “Roof of Africa,” up to 4,550 m (Ras Dashen). - Formation: - Volcanic uplift from East African Rift, 30–40 million years ago. - Significance: - Source of Nile tributaries, biodiversity hub. - Rwenzori Mountains (DRC-Uganda): - - Description: - Peaks at 5,109 m (Margherita). - Formation: - Tectonic uplift along East African Rift, glacial shaping. - Significance: - UNESCO site, unique afro-alpine flora. - Plateaus - Ethiopian Plateau (Ethiopia): - - Description: - ~2,500 m elevation, supports agriculture. - Formation: - Mantle plume uplift during Rift Valley formation. - Significance: - Fertile for coffee, teff cultivation. - Jos Plateau (Nigeria): - - Description: - ~1,500 m, rich in tin. - Formation: - Volcanic activity and erosion of crystalline rocks. - Significance: - Mining hub, agricultural base. - Fouta Djallon Plateau (Guinea): - - Description: - ~1,000 m, river source. - Formation: - Paleozoic orogeny, eroded to stable plateau. - Significance: - Headwaters of Niger, Senegal rivers. - Plains - Serengeti Plains (Tanzania, Kenya): - - Description: - ~30,000 km², wildebeest migration hub. - Formation: - Rift valley sediment deposition, volcanic ash enrichment. - Significance: - Global biodiversity hotspot, tourism. - Niger Delta (Nigeria): - - Description: - ~70,000 km², oil-rich. - Formation: - Alluvial deposition from Niger River. - Significance: - Economic hub, environmental challenges. - Sudanian Savanna (Sahel): - - Description: - Grasslands, Senegal to Sudan. - Formation: - Erosion of plateaus, monsoon rains. - Significance: - Pastoralism, desertification risk. - Deserts - Sahara Desert (North Africa): - - Description: - ~9.2 million km², largest hot desert. - Formation: - Subtropical high-pressure (Hadley cells), Atlas rain shadow. - Significance: - Cultural trade routes, resource exploration. - Kalahari Desert (Botswana, Namibia): - - Description: - ~900,000 km², semi-arid. - Formation: - Rain shadow, limited oceanic moisture. - Significance: - San communities, diamond mining. - Namib Desert (Namibia): - - Description: - ~81,000 km², oldest desert. - Formation: - Cold Benguela Current, inland plateaus. - Significance: - Unique ecosystems, uranium deposits. - Forests - Congo Rainforest (DRC, Congo, Cameroon): - - Description: - ~3.7 million km², second-largest rainforest. - Formation: - ITCZ rainfall, tectonic basins trap moisture. - Significance: - Carbon sink, gorilla habitat. - Ituri Forest (DRC): - - Description: - Northeastern Congo, Mbuti homeland. - Formation: - Equatorial rainfall, low basin elevation. - Significance: - Ethnographic value, biodiversity. - Montane Forests (Ethiopia, Tanzania): - - Description: - Kilimanjaro slopes, Ethiopian Highlands. - Formation: - Orographic rainfall on high elevations. - Significance: - Timber, wild coffee sources. - Major Water Bodies - Rivers - Nile River (Egypt, Sudan, Uganda): - - Description: - ~6,695 km, world’s longest. - Formation: - Drains from tectonic lakes (Victoria) through rift valleys. - Significance: - Lifeline for Egypt, irrigation. - Congo River (DRC, Congo): - - Description: - ~4,700 km, high flow volume. - Formation: - Carved by equatorial rainfall in tectonic basin. - Significance: - Hydropower, transport. - Niger River (Nigeria, Mali): - - Description: - ~4,180 km, West Africa. - Formation: - Drains from Fouta Djallon, alluvial deposition. - Significance: - Agriculture, oil delta. - Lakes - Lake Victoria (Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania): - - Description: - ~68,800 km², second-largest freshwater. - Formation: - Tectonic rift depression, rainfall accumulation. - Significance: - Nile source, fisheries. - Lake Tanganyika (Tanzania, DRC): - - Description: - ~32,900 km², longest freshwater. - Formation: - Deep rift valley, ancient drainage. - Significance: - Unique fish species, trade. - Lake Malawi (Malawi, Mozambique): - - Description: - ~29,600 km², biodiverse. - Formation: - Rift valley depression, tectonic activity. - Significance: - Endemic cichlids, tourism. - Basins - Congo Basin (DRC, Congo): - - Description: - ~3.7 million km², rainforest hub. - Formation: - Tectonic subsidence, sediment accumulation. - Significance: - Biodiversity, carbon storage. - Nile Basin (Egypt, Sudan, Uganda): - - Description: - ~3.4 million km², 11 countries. - Formation: - Rift valley drainage, alluvial deposition. - Significance: - Agriculture, geopolitical tensions. - Chad Basin (Chad, Nigeria): - - Description: - ~2.4 million km², semi-arid. - Formation: - Ancient lakebed, tectonic depression. - Significance: - Oil, shrinking Lake Chad. - Gulfs - Gulf of Guinea (Nigeria, Ghana): - - Description: - ~2.3 million km², shipping hub. - Formation: - Atlantic indentation, tectonic stability. - Significance: - Oil trade, piracy concerns. - Gulf of Aden (Somalia): - - Description: - ~410,000 km², strategic route. - Formation: - Rift between African-Arabian plates. - Significance: - Maritime trade, security. - Islands - Madagascar - - Country: - Madagascar - Description: - ~587,000 km², unique biodiversity - Formation: - Gondwana breakup, tectonic drift. - Seychelles - - Country: - Seychelles - Description: - Granitic islands, ~455 km² - Formation: - Gondwana fragments, tectonic uplift. - Mauritius - - Country: - Mauritius - Description: - Volcanic island, ~2,040 km² - Formation: - Hotspot volcanism, ~8 million years ago. - Comoros - - Country: - Comoros - Description: - Volcanic archipelago, ~1,862 km² - Formation: - East African Rift volcanism. - São Tomé - - Country: - São Tomé and Príncipe - Description: - Volcanic, ~1,001 km² - Formation: - Gulf of Guinea hotspot, ~30 million years. - National Parks/Protected Areas - Serengeti National Park (Tanzania): - - Description: - ~14,750 km², wildebeest migration. - Significance: - UNESCO site, ecotourism. - Kruger National Park (South Africa): - - Description: - ~19,485 km², Big Five wildlife. - Significance: - Conservation, biodiversity hub. - Virunga National Park (DRC): - - Description: - ~7,800 km², mountain gorillas. - Significance: - UNESCO site, conflict zone. - Biodiversity Hotspots - Eastern Afromontane (Ethiopia, Kenya): - - Description: - Highland forests, unique species. - Significance: - Endemic birds, plants; threatened by agriculture. - Madagascar and Indian Ocean Islands: - - Description: - 90% endemic species (e.g., lemurs). - Significance: - Global conservation priority. - Guinean Forests (Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria): - - Description: - Tropical forests, high biodiversity. - Significance: - Threatened by logging, mining. - Human Impact - Deforestation (Congo Basin): - Logging and agriculture reduce forest cover, releasing carbon. - Desertification (Sahel): - Overgrazing and climate change expand arid zones. - Lake Chad Shrinkage: - Irrigation and drought reduce lake size, impacting livelihoods. - Nile Damming: - Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam alters downstream flow, causing geopolitical tensions. - Asia - - Overview - Asia, the largest continent, spans ~44.58 million km², with a population of ~4.7 billion (2023). - It features diverse landscapes, from the Himalayas to the Gobi Desert, shaped by tectonic collisions, monsoon climates, and vast river systems. - Northern Mountains: - - Description: World's highest mountain ranges. - Major Ranges: - Himalayas (India, Nepal, Bhutan, China). - Karakoram (Pakistan, China). - Hindu Kush (Afghanistan). - Tien Shan and Pamirs (Central Asia). - Significance: - Source of major rivers (Ganga, Indus, Yangtze). - Climate barrier (monsoon influence). - Seismic activity due to plate collision (Indian-Eurasian). 2. Central Highlands: - - Description: Rugged plateaus and basins between mountain systems. - Major Features: - Plateau of Tibet (world’s highest). - Iranian Plateau (Iran, Afghanistan). - Anatolian Plateau (Turkey). - Gobi Desert and Mongolian Plateau. - Significance: - Mineral resources. - Harsh climate, sparse population. 3. Southern Plateaus and Peninsulas: - - Description: Stable landmasses forming peninsular Asia. - Major Features: - Deccan Plateau (India). - Arabian Peninsula (Saudi Arabia, etc.). - Indochina Peninsula (Vietnam, Thailand, etc.). - Malay Peninsula. - Significance: - Rich biodiversity. - Monsoonal agriculture. - Oil-rich zones (Arabian region). 4. Great River Plains: - - Description: Fertile lowlands formed by major rivers. - Major Plains: - Indo-Gangetic Plain (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh). - Mesopotamian Plain (Tigris-Euphrates). - North China Plain (Huang He/Yellow River). - Significance: - Densely populated. - Cradle of early civilizations. - Intensive agriculture. 5. Eastern Highlands: - - Description: Mountainous and hilly terrains in East Asia. - Examples: - Great Khingan Mountains (NE China). - Qinling Mountains (China). - Japanese Archipelago Mountains. - Significance: - Earthquake and volcano zones (Pacific Ring of Fire). - Forest and mineral resources. 6. Island Arcs and Archipelagos: - - Description: Chains of islands due to volcanic activity and tectonics. - Major Archipelagos: - Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Andaman & Nicobar. - Features: - Volcanic islands, coral islands. - Significance: - Earthquake-prone. - Marine biodiversity hotspots. 7. Deserts and Arid Zones: - - Major Deserts: - Gobi (Mongolia, China). - Thar (India, Pakistan). - Karakum (Turkmenistan), Kyzylkum (Uzbekistan). - Characteristics: - Low rainfall. - Sparse vegetation and habitation. - Economic Use: - Nomadic herding, mineral extraction. 8. Coastal Regions and Deltas: - - Major Deltas: - Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta (world’s largest). - Mekong Delta (Vietnam). - Yangtze Delta (China). - Coastal Features: - Estuaries, lagoons, mangroves. - Importance: - Ports, trade centers, agriculture, fisheries. - Formation: - Tectonic collisions (e.g., India-Eurasia) formed mountains and plateaus; erosion and deposition created plains; arid climates shaped deserts. - South America, the fourth-largest continent, spans ~17.84 million km², with a population of ~430 million (2023). - It features diverse landscapes, from the Andes to the Amazon Rainforest, shaped by tectonic subduction, equatorial climates, and vast river systems. - Coastal reclamation degrades mangroves, coral reefs. - Arctic Region - - Overview - The Arctic Region, spanning ~14 million km² across the Arctic Ocean and surrounding landmasses, has a transient population of ~4 million (2023). It features ice-covered seas, tundra, and permafrost, shaped by glacial cycles, polar climate, and emerging geopolitical interests. - Countries (0 recognized sovereign states) - None - Territories of 8 Arctic Council nations: Canada, Denmark (Greenland), Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, United States (Alaska). Governed by international agreements like UNCLOS and the Arctic Council. - Physiographic Divisions - The Arctic’s landscape is divided into three regions: 1. Arctic Ocean Basin: - - Description: - Ice-covered ocean, deep basins. - Location: - Central Arctic. - Climate: - Polar (EF in Köppen), extreme cold. - Features: - Sea ice, underwater ridges. - Countries: - None (international waters, claimed by Canada, Russia, Denmark). 2. Global Oceans - - Overview - Global Oceans, covering ~361 million km² (71% of Earth’s surface), have no permanent population but support ~3 billion coastal residents (2023). They include the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic Oceans, shaping climate, biodiversity, and global trade. - Countries (Key coastal nations with governance roles) - None (sovereign states govern coastal zones, exclusive economic zones under UNCLOS) - Pacific: United States, Japan, Australia, Indonesia - Atlantic: Brazil, Canada, Nigeria, United Kingdom - Indian: India, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Maldives - Southern: Chile, Argentina, New Zealand - Arctic: Canada, Russia, Norway, Denmark (Greenland) - Physiographic Divisions - - Global Oceans are divided into five major oceans: 1. Pacific Ocean: - Description: - Largest ocean, ~155 million km². - Location: - Between Americas, Asia, Australia. - Climate: - Tropical to polar. - Features: - Mariana Trench, coral reefs. - Countries: - United States, Japan, Indonesia, Australia. 2. Atlantic Ocean: - Description: - ~86 million km², second largest. - Location: - Between Americas, Europe, Africa. - Climate: - Temperate to polar. - Features: - Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Gulf Stream. - Countries: - Brazil, Canada, Nigeria, United Kingdom. 3. Indian Ocean: - Description: - ~70 million km², third largest. - Location: - Between Africa, Asia, Australia. - Climate: - Tropical, monsoon-influenced. - Features: - Seychelles Plateau, monsoonal currents. - Countries: - India, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Maldives. 4. Southern Ocean: - Description: - ~20 million km², encircles Antarctica. - Location: - Southern Hemisphere, below 60°S. - Climate: - Polar, stormy. - Features: - Antarctic Circumpolar Current, icebergs. - Countries: - Chile, Argentina, New Zealand. 5. Arctic Ocean: - Description: - ~14 million km², smallest ocean. - Location: - North Polar region. - Climate: - Polar, ice-covered. - Features: - Sea ice, Lomonosov Ridge. - Countries: - Canada, Russia, Norway, Denmark. - Formation: - Tectonic plate divergence formed ocean basins; continental drift shaped boundaries; glacial cycles influenced sea levels and currents. - Major Physical Features - Mountain Ranges - Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Atlantic): - - Description: - ~16,000 km, submarine ridge. - Formation: - Seafloor spreading, tectonic divergence. - Significance: - Volcanic activity, new crust formation. - East Pacific Rise (Pacific): - - Description: - ~10,000 km, fast-spreading ridge. - Formation: - Tectonic divergence, volcanic. - Significance: - Earthquake zone, marine ecosystems. - Carlsberg Ridge (Indian): - - Description: - ~3,000 km, submarine ridge. - Formation: - Seafloor spreading, tectonic. - Significance: - Deep-sea vents, biodiversity. - Plateaus - Seychelles Plateau (Indian): - - Description: - ~40,000 km², submerged granite. - Formation: - Continental fragment, tectonic drift. - Significance: - Coral reefs, fisheries. - Kerguelen Plateau (Southern): - - Description: - ~1.2 million km², volcanic plateau. - Formation: - Hotspot volcanism, tectonic. - Significance: - Marine biodiversity, research. - Ontong Java Plateau (Pacific): - - Description: - ~1.5 million km², submarine. - Formation: - Volcanic eruptions, Cretaceous. - Significance: - Carbon sink, geological study. - Deserts - No terrestrial deserts; oceanic deserts exist as low-productivity zones. - South Pacific Gyre (Pacific): - - Description: - ~37 million km², nutrient-poor. - Formation: - Ocean circulation, low upwelling. - Significance: - Low biodiversity, plastic accumulation. - Forests - No terrestrial forests; marine equivalents exist. - Kelp Forests (Pacific, Atlantic, Southern): - - Description: - ~100,000 km², coastal ecosystems. - Formation: - Cold, nutrient-rich waters. - Significance: - Marine biodiversity, fisheries. - Major Water Bodies - Rivers - No rivers in oceans; coastal rivers influence marine systems. - Lakes - No lakes in oceans; subglacial lakes noted in Arctic/Southern. - Lake Vostok (Southern, under Antarctic ice): - - Description: - ~12,500 km², subglacial. - Formation: - Tectonic depression, ice cover. - Significance: - Ancient microbes, climate data. - Islands - Hawaii - - Country: - United States - Description: - ~28,311 km², volcanic archipelago. - Formation: - Hotspot volcanism, Pacific plate. - Iceland - - Country: - Iceland - Description: - ~103,000 km², volcanic. - Formation: - Mid-Atlantic Ridge, tectonic. - Maldives - - Country: - Maldives - Description: - ~298 km², coral atolls. - Formation: - Coral growth, submerged volcanoes. - South Georgia - - Country: - United Kingdom - Description: - ~3,903 km², sub-Antarctic. - Formation: - Tectonic uplift, glacial erosion. - Svalbard - - Country: - Norway - Description: - ~61,022 km², polar archipelago. - Formation: - Tectonic uplift, glacial carving. - National Parks/Protected Areas - Great Barrier Reef Marine Park (Pacific, Australia): - - Description: - ~344,400 km², coral reef system. - Significance: - UNESCO site, marine biodiversity. - Galápagos Marine Reserve (Pacific, Ecuador): - - Description: - ~133,000 km², oceanic ecosystem. - Significance: - Endemic species, ecotourism. - Wadden Sea (Atlantic, Netherlands, Germany, Denmark): - - Description: - ~11,500 km², tidal flats. - Significance: - UNESCO site, migratory birds. - Biodiversity Hotspots - Coral Triangle (Pacific, Indian): - - Description: - ~6 million km², marine ecosystems. - Significance: - Highest coral diversity, overfishing threat. - Sargasso Sea (Atlantic): - - Description: - ~5 million km², floating seaweed. - Significance: - Eel breeding, plastic pollution. - Southern Ocean Ecosystems (Southern): - - Description: - ~20 million km², polar marine. - Significance: - Krill, climate change impact. - Human Impact - Plastic Pollution (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian): - Marine debris harms ecosystems, accumulates in gyres. - Overfishing (All Oceans): - Unsustainable fishing depletes stocks, disrupts food webs. - Coral Bleaching (Pacific, Indian): - Climate change and warming waters degrade reefs. - Arctic Ice Melt (Arctic): - Warming opens shipping routes, threatens polar habitats.
- Physical Geography PYQs - [1995] - Q1: A meteor is: - Options: (a) a rapidly moving star (b) a piece of matter which has entered the earth's atmosphere from outer space (c) part of a constellation (d) a comet without a tail - Answer: (b) a piece of matter which has entered the earth's atmosphere from outer space - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - A meteor is a fragment of rock or metal (meteoroid) from space that enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up due to friction, creating a visible streak of light (often called a "shooting star"). - This phenomenon occurs when meteoroids, typically from comets or asteroids, encounter Earth's atmosphere at high speeds (10-70 km/s), distinguishing them from other celestial bodies. - Why Not Others?: - (a) A rapidly moving star: - Incorrect—Stars are massive, luminous bodies fixed in their positions relative to Earth over short timescales. A "rapidly moving star" is a misnomer; the visible motion of meteors is due to their atmospheric entry, not stellar movement. - (c) Part of a constellation: - Incorrect—Constellations are patterns of stars as seen from Earth, fixed in the night sky. Meteors are transient phenomena unrelated to these patterns. - (d) A comet without a tail: - Incorrect—Comets are icy bodies that develop tails when heated by the Sun, but a meteor is a distinct object (a meteoroid burning up). Even a comet without a visible tail is not a meteor. - Related Concepts: - Meteoroid: - The solid object in space before entering the atmosphere. - Meteor: - The visible streak during atmospheric entry. - Meteorite: - A meteoroid that survives and lands on Earth’s surface. - Meteor Showers: - Events like the Perseids or Leonids, caused by Earth passing through comet debris, producing multiple meteors. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on astronomy (e.g., Q84 [2012-I] on celestial bodies) or atmospheric phenomena, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of physical geography in UPSC exams. - Understanding meteors ties into broader topics like planetary science or the study of near-Earth objects (NEOs). - Key Takeaway: - A meteor is specifically the visible phenomenon of a meteoroid burning in Earth’s atmosphere, distinct from stars, constellations, or comets, highlighting precise astronomical terminology. - Q3: The graph given below shows the mean average monthly temperatures (in °C) and mean monthly rainfall (in cm) of a place: - - This graph is indicative of which one of the climatic zones of the world? - Options: (a) Wet and dry tropical (b) Rainy tropical (c) Semi-arid tropical (d) Temperate marine - Answer: (a) Wet and dry tropical - Q4: Willy Willy is: - Options: (a) a type of tree grown in temperate regions (b) a wind that blows in a desert (c) a tropical cyclone of the North-west Australia (d) a kind of common fish found near Laccadive Islands - Answer: (c) a tropical cyclone of the North-west Australia - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - A Willy Willy is a local term for a tropical cyclone in North-west Australia, particularly affecting coastal areas of Western Australia and the Northern Territory. - These cyclones form over warm ocean waters (above 26.5°C) in the Indian Ocean and Timor Sea, typically between November and April, bringing heavy rain, strong winds, and storm surges. - Why Not Others?: - (a) A type of tree grown in temperate regions: - Incorrect—No evidence links "Willy Willy" to trees; the term is meteorological, not botanical. - (b) A wind that blows in a desert: - Incorrect—While Australia has desert winds (e.g., dust storms), Willy Willy specifically refers to tropical cyclones, not arid winds. - (d) A kind of common fish found near Laccadive Islands: - Incorrect—Willy Willy is unrelated to marine biology or the Laccadive (Lakshadweep) Islands, which are in the Arabian Sea. - Related Concepts: - Tropical Cyclones: - Known by different names globally: hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (Pacific), cyclones (Indian Ocean). - Other Regional Terms: - Cyclone (India/Bangladesh), Baguios (Philippines), Taifu (Japan). - Australian Cyclones: - Notable examples include Cyclone Tracy (1974), which devastated Darwin. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on meteorological phenomena (e.g., Q29 [2001] on local winds like Fohn) or natural disasters (e.g., Q18 [1998] on Indonesian fires). - Understanding cyclone terminology is crucial for studying climate impacts and disaster management in geography. - Key Takeaway: - Willy Willy is a regional term for tropical cyclones in North-west Australia, distinguishing it from other meteorological or biological phenomena. - Q5: Which one of the following is the continent with the highest mean elevation in the world? - Options: (a) Antarctica (b) North America (c) Asia (d) South America - Answer: (a) Antarctica - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - Antarctica has the highest mean elevation of any continent, averaging about 2,300 meters above sea level, due to its massive ice sheet, which is up to 4 km thick in places. - This elevation is driven by the thick ice covering 98% of the continent, elevating its surface far above sea level, unlike other continents with varied topography. - Why Not Others?: - (b) North America: - Incorrect—North America’s mean elevation is about 720 meters, with high points like the Rockies (e.g., Mt. Elbert, 4,401 m) but lower overall due to vast plains. - (c) Asia: - Incorrect—Asia, with the Himalayas (e.g., Everest, 8,848 m), has a mean elevation of about 950 meters, lowered by extensive lowlands like the Ganges Plain. - (d) South America: - Incorrect—South America’s mean elevation is around 590 meters, with the Andes (e.g., Aconcagua, 6,960 m) but significant lowlands like the Amazon Basin. - Elevation Data: - Antarctica: ~2,300 m (ice-driven, highest due to ice sheet). - Asia: ~950 m (Himalayas offset by lowlands). - North America: ~720 m (Rockies, plains balance). - South America: ~590 m (Andes, Amazon lowlands). - Related Concepts: - Ice Sheets: - Antarctica’s elevation is due to its ice sheet, unlike Greenland’s smaller ice cover. - Plate Tectonics: - Other continents’ elevations are influenced by tectonic activity (e.g., Andes, Himalayas), but Antarctica’s is ice-dominated. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on physical geography (e.g., Q52 [2005] on continental land area) or polar environments (e.g., Q88 [2018-I] on shrinking water bodies). - Understanding elevation impacts climate, glaciation, and global sea level studies. - Key Takeaway: - Antarctica’s unparalleled mean elevation, driven by its ice sheet, sets it apart from other continents, a critical fact in physical geography. - [1996] - Q6: Which one of the following layers of the atmosphere is responsible for the deflection of radio waves? - Options: (a) Troposphere (b) Stratosphere (c) Mesosphere (d) Ionosphere - Answer: (d) Ionosphere - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - The ionosphere, located 50-1000 km above Earth’s surface, contains charged particles (ions) due to solar radiation. It deflects radio waves, enabling long-distance communication by reflecting shortwave radio signals back to Earth. - This is vital for radio broadcasting and early global communication, as signals can bounce over the horizon. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Troposphere: - Incorrect—The troposphere (0-12 km) is where weather occurs, with water vapor and neutral gases, but lacks ionization to deflect radio waves. - (b) Stratosphere: - Incorrect—The stratosphere (12-50 km), containing the ozone layer, absorbs UV radiation but has no significant ionization for radio wave reflection. - (c) Mesosphere: - Incorrect—The mesosphere (50-85 km) is thin, with minimal ionization, unsuitable for radio wave deflection compared to the ionosphere. - Related Concepts: - Ionospheric Layers: - Includes D, E, and F layers; the F-layer is key for reflecting high-frequency radio waves during the day. - Solar Activity: - Solar flares increase ionization, enhancing reflection but potentially disrupting signals (e.g., radio blackouts). - Broader Connection: - Links to atmospheric science questions (e.g., Q57 [2006] on geographical phenomena) or communication technology, showing the ionosphere’s role in physical geography. - Relevant to space weather impacts on GPS and satellite systems. - Key Takeaway: - The ionosphere’s ionized particles enable radio wave deflection, a unique function critical for communication, distinct from other atmospheric layers. - Q7: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R): - Assertion (A): Areas near the equator receive rainfall throughout the year. - Reason (R): High temperatures and high humidity cause convectional rain in most afternoons near the equator. - In the context of the above two statements, which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - Equatorial regions (e.g., Amazon Basin, Congo Basin, Indonesia) have a rainy tropical climate (Af in Köppen classification), with 200-400 cm of rainfall yearly due to the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), where trade winds converge, causing uplift and precipitation. - High temperatures (25-30°C) and humidity drive convectional rainfall, where warm, moist air rises, cools, and condenses, forming afternoon showers or thunderstorms. - Assertion (A) Analysis: - True—Equatorial areas receive near-daily rainfall, with no pronounced dry season, due to consistent ITCZ activity. - Reason (R) Analysis: - True—High temperatures and humidity cause convectional rain, as heated air creates low-pressure systems, leading to regular afternoon precipitation. - Correct Explanation—R explains A, as convectional rain is the primary mechanism for year-round equatorial rainfall. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R directly explains A, as convectional rain drives the consistent rainfall. - (c) A is true but R is false: - Incorrect—R is true; convectional rain is a well-documented equatorial phenomenon. - (d) A is false but R is true: - Incorrect—A is true; equatorial regions do receive year-round rainfall. - Related Concepts: - ITCZ: - A low-pressure zone driving equatorial rainfall, shifting slightly with seasons. - Convectional Rainfall: - Common in tropics, linked to daily heating cycles, unlike frontal or orographic rain. - Broader Connection: - Links to climatic zone questions (e.g., Q3 [1995] on tropical climates) or atmospheric processes, relevant for understanding global weather patterns in UPSC geography. - Key Takeaway: - Equatorial rainfall is driven by convectional processes due to high temperatures and humidity, making both the assertion and its explanation accurate. - Q8: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R): - Assertion (A): Mangroves are very specialised forest ecosystems of tropical and sub-tropical regions bordering certain sea coasts. - Reason (R): They stabilise the shoreline and act as bulwark against encroachments by the sea. - In the context of the above two statements, which one of the following is correct? - Options: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - Mangroves are specialized forest ecosystems found in tropical and subtropical coastal regions (e.g., Sunderbans, Andaman and Nicobar Islands), thriving in saline, tidal zones with waterlogged soils. - They have specialized adaptations such as aerial roots (pneumatophores) and salt-filtering mechanisms, supporting a rich biodiversity of fish, birds, and crustaceans. - Assertion (A) Analysis: - True—Mangroves are unique ecosystems in tropical/subtropical coastal areas, shaped by environmental conditions and biological adaptations. - Reason (R) Analysis: - True—Mangroves stabilize shorelines by trapping sediment with their dense root systems, reducing erosion, and acting as natural barriers against sea surges and tsunamis. - Correct Explanation—Their ability to stabilise shorelines and protect against sea encroachment directly supports their ecological role, explaining why they are so specialised in such coastal environments. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R *does* help explain A, since shoreline protection is a direct result of mangrove adaptations. - (c) A is true but R is false: - Incorrect—R is factually correct; mangroves do act as natural coastal bulwarks. - (d) A is false but R is true: - Incorrect—A is factually true and widely accepted. - Related Concepts: - Mangrove Adaptations: - Viviparous seeds, salt-excreting leaves, stilt and pneumatophore roots for oxygen intake in anoxic mud. - Ecological Roles: - Serve as breeding grounds for marine species, carbon sequestration hubs, and buffers against climate-related disasters. - Broader Connection: - Ties into questions on biosphere reserves (e.g., Q2 [1995] – Sunderbans) and coastal ecosystems (e.g., Q31 [2001] – Gulf of Mannar). - Highly relevant to environmental geography and climate resilience themes. - Key Takeaway: - Mangroves are specialized due to both their ecological adaptations and functional role in shoreline protection, making R a correct and relevant explanation of A. - Q9: Diamond ring is a phenomenon observed: - Options: (a) at the start of a total solar eclipse (b) at the end of a total solar eclipse (c) only along the peripheral regions of the totality trail (d) only in the central regions of the totality trail - Answer: (c) only along the peripheral regions of the totality trail - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - The diamond ring effect is a brief flash of bright light seen during a total solar eclipse. - It occurs when a tiny portion of the Sun's photosphere shines through lunar valleys just before or just after totality, creating a brilliant point of light — like a diamond — on the ring of the Sun’s corona. - This is most clearly visible near the start or end of the total eclipse, which corresponds to the peripheral regions within the totality path. - Assertion Analysis: - The effect does not occur outside the path of totality — hence, it’s not visible during partial eclipses. - It also doesn’t occur during the central part of totality, where the Sun is fully blocked. - Therefore, the phenomenon is best observed along the inner edges (peripheral areas) of the totality trail — making option (c) accurate. - Why Not Others?: - (a) At the start of a total solar eclipse: - Partially true — it may occur, but the question specifies exclusivity, and it's not limited to the start alone. - (b) At the end of a total solar eclipse: - Also partially true, but again not exclusive. - (d) Only in the central regions of the totality trail: - Incorrect — the central region has full totality with no visible photosphere, so no diamond ring. - Related Concepts: - Baily’s Beads: - Precede or follow the diamond ring effect due to sunlight passing through lunar valleys. - Totality Path: - The narrow area on Earth’s surface where a total solar eclipse is visible. Diamond ring occurs only within this path, near the edges. - Broader Connection: - Relevant to astronomy and physical geography. - Also appears in UPSC questions involving celestial phenomena, optics, or eclipse mechanics. - Key Takeaway: - The diamond ring effect occurs specifically along the peripheral regions of the path of totality, just before or after totality — making option (c) the most accurate answer. - [1997] - Q10: Which one of the following factors is responsible for the change in the regular direction of the ocean currents in the Indian Ocean? - Options: (a) Indian Ocean is half an ocean (b) Indian Ocean has monsoon drift (c) Indian Ocean is a land-locked ocean (d) Indian Ocean has greater variation in salinity - Answer: (b) Indian Ocean has monsoon drift - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - The Indian Ocean’s currents reverse seasonally due to the monsoon, a unique phenomenon called monsoon drift. During the southwest monsoon (June-September), winds push surface currents northeastward; during the northeast monsoon (November-February), they reverse southwestward. - This is driven by monsoon winds, influenced by the differential heating of the Indian subcontinent and surrounding ocean. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Indian Ocean is half an ocean: - Incorrect—No standard geographical definition supports this; the Indian Ocean is a full ocean, smaller than the Pacific or Atlantic but not “half.” - (c) Indian Ocean is a land-locked ocean: - Incorrect—The Indian Ocean is not land-locked; it connects to the Pacific and Atlantic via open boundaries, unlike the Mediterranean. - (d) Indian Ocean has greater variation in salinity: - Incorrect—Salinity variations exist but are not the primary driver of current reversals, which are wind-driven by monsoons. - Related Concepts: - Monsoon Winds: - Seasonal wind reversals due to land-ocean temperature contrasts, affecting currents and rainfall. - Other Currents: - North Equatorial Current and South Equatorial Current are influenced by monsoons, unlike steady currents like the Gulf Stream. - Broader Connection: - Links to oceanography questions (e.g., Q43 [2004] on Mekong River) or monsoon impacts (e.g., Q7 [1996] on equatorial rainfall). - Relevant to climate studies, as monsoon currents affect fishing, navigation, and coastal economies. - Key Takeaway: - Monsoon drift, driven by seasonal wind reversals, uniquely alters Indian Ocean currents, distinguishing it from other oceans. - Q11: Daily weather map showing isobars is an example of: - Options: (a) Choropleth map (b) Isopleth map (c) Chorochromatic map (d) Choroschematic map - Answer: (b) Isopleth map - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - An isopleth map displays lines (isopleths) connecting points of equal value, such as isobars (equal atmospheric pressure) on a weather map. Daily weather maps use isobars to show pressure systems, aiding in forecasting. - Isobars indicate high-pressure (anticyclones) and low-pressure (cyclones) areas, critical for meteorology. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Choropleth map: - Incorrect—Choropleth maps show data variations across regions (e.g., population density) using shaded areas, not continuous lines like isobars. - (c) Chorochromatic map: - Incorrect—These maps use colors to show categorical data (e.g., soil types), not numerical values like pressure. - (d) Choroschematic map: - Incorrect—These use symbols to represent features (e.g., crop types), not lines for equal values. - Related Concepts: - Other Isopleths: - Isotherms (temperature), isohyets (rainfall), contour lines (elevation). - Weather Maps: - Include fronts, wind patterns, and precipitation, with isobars as a key feature. - Broader Connection: - Links to meteorology questions (e.g., Q4 [1995] on Willy Willy) or cartography, essential for understanding weather patterns in UPSC geography. - Relevant to climate analysis and disaster preparedness. - Key Takeaway: - Isopleth maps, like those with isobars, represent continuous data (pressure) with lines, distinguishing them from other map types. - Q12: The group of small pieces of rock revolving round the sun between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter are called: - Options: (a) meteors (b) comets (c) meteorites (d) asteroids - Answer: (d) asteroids - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Asteroids are rocky bodies orbiting the Sun, primarily in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter (2.1-3.3 AU). They range from small rocks to large bodies like Ceres (a dwarf planet). - The belt contains millions of asteroids, remnants of the solar system’s formation, distinct from other celestial objects. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Meteors: - Incorrect—Meteors are meteoroids burning up in Earth’s atmosphere, not orbiting bodies (see Q1 [1995]). - (b) Comets: - Incorrect—Comets are icy bodies with elliptical orbits, developing tails near the Sun, not confined to the asteroid belt. - (c) Meteorites: - Incorrect—Meteorites are meteoroids that land on Earth, not orbiting objects. - Related Concepts: - Asteroid Belt: - Formed from material that failed to coalesce into a planet due to Jupiter’s gravity. - Notable Asteroids: - Ceres, Vesta, Pallas; some are studied for mining potential. - Broader Connection: - Links to astronomy questions (e.g., Q1 [1995] on meteors) or solar system dynamics, relevant for physical geography and space exploration. - Ties to near-Earth asteroid tracking for planetary defense. - Key Takeaway: - Asteroids, orbiting in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, are distinct rocky bodies, unlike meteors, comets, or meteorites. - Q13: If the earth's direction of rotation is reversed, what should be the IST when it is noon at the International Date Line? - Options: (a) 06.30 hrs (b) 05.30 hrs (c) 18.30 hrs (d) 17.30 hrs - Answer: (a) 06.30 hrs - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Earth normally rotates from west to east, which makes places to the east (like India at 82.5°E) ahead in time compared to places to the west (like the International Date Line at 180°). - In this natural direction, when it is noon at the IDL, it is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead in IST, i.e., 17:30 hrs. - If the Earth’s rotation is reversed (i.e., east to west), the time progression also reverses — now, places west of the IDL (like India) would be behind in time instead of ahead. - Thus, when it is noon at the IDL, India would be 5.5 hours behind, making the IST 06:30 hrs. - Why Not Others?: - (b) 05.30 hrs: - Incorrect—It suggests a 6.5-hour difference, not the correct 5.5 hours. - (c) 18.30 hrs: - Incorrect—That would be the time in India if Earth rotated in the usual direction and India was 6.5 hours ahead, not behind. - (d) 17.30 hrs: - Incorrect—Matches regular rotation, not reversed rotation. - Related Concepts: - Earth’s Rotation and Time Zones: - Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, i.e., 15° per hour. Time zones are calculated based on this. - Reversal of rotation flips the direction of time zone advancement. - International Date Line: - Serves as the boundary for calendar dates and lies opposite the Prime Meridian. - Broader Connection: - Helpful for UPSC questions dealing with physical geography, time zones, Earth’s rotation, and global navigation. - Key Takeaway: - Reversing Earth’s rotation causes a reversal in time zone relationships. Therefore, if it is noon at the IDL, Indian Standard Time (IST) would be 06:30 hrs, as India would now be 5.5 hours behind, not ahead. - Q14: Which one of the following stars is nearest to the Earth? - Options: (a) Polaris (b) Alpha Centauri (c) Sun (d) Sirius - Answer: (c) Sun - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - The Sun, at an average distance of 149.6 million km (1 AU), is Earth’s closest star, providing light, heat, and energy essential for life. - Other stars are much farther, measured in light-years (1 ly ≈ 9.46 trillion km). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Polaris: - Incorrect—Polaris (North Star) is ~433 light-years away, used for navigation but not close. - (b) Alpha Centauri: - Incorrect—Alpha Centauri, the closest star system after the Sun, is 4.37 light-years away, including Proxima Centauri (4.24 ly). - (d) Sirius: - Incorrect—Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, is 8.6 light-years away. - Related Concepts: - Stellar Distances: - Measured in light-years or parsecs (1 pc = 3.26 ly). - Closest Stars: - Proxima Centauri is the nearest after the Sun, part of the Alpha Centauri system. - Broader Connection: - Links to astronomy questions (e.g., Q9 [1996] on solar eclipses) or celestial navigation, vital for physical geography. - Relevant to solar system studies and astrophysics. - Key Takeaway: - The Sun, as Earth’s closest star, is uniquely significant, far nearer than other stars like Alpha Centauri or Sirius. - Q15: Which one of the following conditions is most relevant for the presence of life on Mars? - Options: (a) Atmospheric composition (b) Thermal conditions (c) Occurrence of ice caps and frozen water (d) Occurrence of ozone - Answer: (c) Occurrence of ice caps and frozen water - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Life, as understood from Earth, requires liquid water, a key factor for habitability. Mars has polar ice caps and subsurface frozen water, confirmed by missions like Viking and Mars Odyssey, suggesting potential past or present liquid water. - While atmospheric composition and temperature are important, water availability is the most critical for life, as it supports biochemical processes. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Atmospheric composition: - Incorrect—Mars’ atmosphere is thin (0.6% Earth’s pressure), mostly CO₂ (95%), with little oxygen, less critical than water for life. - (b) Thermal conditions: - Incorrect—Mars’ temperatures (-140°C to 20°C) are harsh, but extremophiles could survive; water remains more essential. - (d) Occurrence of ozone: - Incorrect—Mars lacks significant ozone, offering little UV protection, but this is less critical than water for life’s existence. - Related Concepts: - Martian Water: - Evidence includes polar caps, subsurface ice, and past riverbeds, suggesting a wetter past. - Astrobiology: - Searches for microbial life focus on water-rich areas, like recurring slope lineae (RSL). - Broader Connection: - Links to planetary science questions (e.g., Q12 [1997] on asteroids) or exobiology, relevant for UPSC’s focus on space exploration. - Ties to NASA’s Perseverance mission seeking signs of ancient life. - Key Takeaway: - Frozen water on Mars, via ice caps and subsurface ice, is the most relevant condition for potential life, surpassing atmospheric or thermal factors. - Q16: Consider the map given below: - - Of the four shaded areas in the map, which is characterised by hot dry summers, mild and moist winters and seasonal reversal of winds? - Options: (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4 - Answer: (a) 1 - [1998] - Q17: Consider the following statements regarding asteroids: - Statements: 1. Asteroids are rocky debris of varying size orbiting the sun 2. Most of the asteroids are small but some have diameter as large as 1000 km 3. The orbit of asteroids lies between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn - Of these statements: - Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 are correct (b) 2 and 3 are correct (c) 1 and 2 are correct (d) 1 and 3 are correct - Answer: (c) 1 and 2 are correct - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Asteroids are rocky, airless bodies orbiting the Sun, primarily in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter (2.1-3.3 AU), remnants of the solar system’s formation. - Statement 1: True—Asteroids are rocky debris, ranging from meters to hundreds of kilometers. - Statement 2: True—Most asteroids are small, but some, like Ceres (~940 km diameter), approach 1000 km. - Statement 3: False—The asteroid belt is between Mars and Jupiter, not Jupiter and Saturn (5.2-9.5 AU). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1, 2, and 3 are correct: - Incorrect—Statement 3 is false, as asteroids orbit between Mars and Jupiter. - (b) 2 and 3 are correct: - Incorrect—Statement 3 is false. - (d) 1 and 3 are correct: - Incorrect—Statement 3 is false. - Related Concepts: - Asteroid Belt: - Contains millions of asteroids, shaped by Jupiter’s gravity (see Q12 [1997]). - Notable Asteroids: - Ceres (dwarf planet), Vesta, Pallas; studied for resources. - Broader Connection: - Links to astronomy questions (e.g., Q12 [1997] on asteroids) or solar system dynamics, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to planetary defense against near-Earth asteroids. - Key Takeaway: - Asteroids are rocky bodies in the Mars-Jupiter belt, with sizes up to ~1000 km, but not between Jupiter and Saturn. - Q18: Match the rivers labelled A, B, C and D on the given map with their names given in the list and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: - List-I - - List-II: 1. St. Lawrence 2. Orinoco 3. Mackenzie 4. Amazon 5. Yukon - Options: (a) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1 (b) A-5, B-3, C-1, D-2 (c) A-5, B-4, C-1, D-3 (d) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 - Answer: (b) A-5, B-3, C-1, D-2 - Q19: The correct sequence of different layers of the atmosphere from the surface of the Earth upwards is: - Options: (a) Troposphere, Stratosphere, Ionosphere, Mesosphere (b) Stratosphere, Troposphere, Ionosphere, Mesosphere (c) Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Ionosphere (d) Stratosphere, Troposphere, Mesosphere, Ionosphere - Answer: (c) Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Ionosphere - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Earth’s atmosphere is layered by temperature and composition: - Troposphere (0-12 km): Weather layer, temperature decreases. - Stratosphere (12-50 km): Ozone layer, temperature increases. - Mesosphere (50-85 km): Coldest, meteors burn up. - Ionosphere (50-1000 km, overlapping mesosphere/thermosphere): Ionized, reflects radio waves (see Q6 [1996]). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Troposphere, Stratosphere, Ionosphere, Mesosphere: - Incorrect—Ionosphere extends beyond mesosphere, not before. - (b) Stratosphere, Troposphere, Ionosphere, Mesosphere: - Incorrect—Troposphere is lowest, not stratosphere. - (d) Stratosphere, Troposphere, Mesosphere, Ionosphere: - Incorrect—Troposphere is first, not stratosphere. - Related Concepts: - Thermosphere: - Above mesosphere (85-600 km), includes part of ionosphere, hosts auroras. - Exosphere: - Outermost layer, transitions to space. - Broader Connection: - Links to atmospheric science (e.g., Q6 [1996] on ionosphere) or meteorology, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to climate and satellite communication. - Key Takeaway: - Atmospheric layers, from surface up, are Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Ionosphere, each with distinct roles. - Q20: Estuaries possess distinct blooms of excessive growth of a pigmented dinoflagellates. These blooms are called: - Options: (a) red tides (b) sea tides (c) black tides (d) sea flowers - Answer: (a) red tides - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Red tides are blooms of pigmented dinoflagellates (e.g., Karenia brevis) in estuaries/coastal waters, causing reddish discoloration due to high cell concentrations. - These can produce toxins, harming marine life and humans (e.g., shellfish poisoning), often triggered by nutrient runoff. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Sea tides: - Incorrect—Sea tides are gravitational, not biological phenomena. - (c) Black tides: - Incorrect—Black tides refer to oil spills, not algal blooms. - (d) Sea flowers: - Incorrect—No such term for dinoflagellate blooms; a misnomer. - Related Concepts: - Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs): - Red tides are HABs, impacting fisheries and ecosystems. - Eutrophication: - Nutrient enrichment (nitrogen, phosphorus) fuels blooms. - Broader Connection: - Links to environmental science (e.g., Q2 [1995] on biosphere reserves) or marine ecology, key for UPSC geography. - Relevant to coastal pollution and ecosystem management. - Key Takeaway: - Red tides, caused by dinoflagellate blooms, are significant in estuaries, distinct from tidal or oil-related phenomena. - Q21: Consider the following climatic conditions (northern hemisphere): - Temp. °C Rainfall cm. J 3.9 4.7 F 4.4 5.7 M 8.3 8.2 A 14.4 9.2 M 20.0 9.2 J 23.3 17.7 J 27.8 14.5 A 27.8 14.0 S 22.3 12.7 O 18.3 7.0 N 12.2 5.0 D 6.7 3.5 - These are most likely to be found in the natural regions of: - Options: (a) China type (b) equatorial type (c) hot desert type (d) monsoon type - Answer: (a) China type - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - China type climate (Cwa/Cwb, Köppen), in eastern China, southeast USA, and parts of Argentina, has warm, humid summers (hottest ~27.8°C) and mild, drier winters (~3.9°C), with summer rainfall peaks (June: 17.7 cm). - Data shows high summer temperatures/rainfall, cooler/drier winters, matching China type due to monsoon and continental influences. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Equatorial type: - Incorrect—Equatorial (Af) has consistent high temperatures (~25-30°C) and rainfall year-round, not seasonal (see Q7 [1996]). - (c) Hot desert type: - Incorrect—Deserts (BWh) have high temperatures but low rainfall (<25 cm/year), unlike ~111.2 cm here. - (d) Monsoon type: - Incorrect—Monsoon (Am/As) has stronger wet seasons; data’s milder winters align better with China type. - Related Concepts: - Köppen Cwa: - Cold, dry winter; warmest month under 32°C. - Similar Regions: - Southeast USA (Georgia), eastern Australia (Queensland). - Broader Connection: - Links to climatic zones (e.g., Q7 [1996] on equatorial rainfall) or agriculture, key for UPSC geography. - Relevant to monsoon-influenced temperate climates. - Key Takeaway: - China type climate, with warm, wet summers and mild, drier winters, matches the data, distinct from equatorial, desert, or monsoon climates. - Q22: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer by using the codes given below the lists: - List-I (Special characteristic): A. Smallest planet of the solar system B. Largest planet of the solar system C. Planet second from the Sun in the solar system D. Planet nearest to the Sun - List-II (Name of planet): 1. Mercury 2. Venus 3. Jupiter 4. Pluto 5. Saturn - Options: (a) A-2, B-3, C-5, D-1 (b) A-3, B-5, C-1, D-2 (c) A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3 (d) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1 - Answer: (d) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1 - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - In 1998, Pluto was a planet (reclassified as dwarf planet in 2006). Matches: - A. Smallest: Pluto (~2,377 km diameter). - B. Largest: Jupiter (~139,820 km). - C. Second from Sun: Venus (after Mercury). - D. Nearest to Sun: Mercury. - Correct: A-4 (Pluto), B-3 (Jupiter), C-2 (Venus), D-1 (Mercury). - Why Not Others?: - (a) A-2, B-3, C-5, D-1: - Incorrect—Venus not smallest; Saturn not second. - (b) A-3, B-5, C-1, D-2: - Incorrect—Jupiter not smallest; Mercury not second; Venus not nearest. - (c) A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3: - Incorrect—Mercury not largest; Jupiter not nearest. - Related Concepts: - Planetary Order: - Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, (Pluto). - Size: - Jupiter > Saturn > Uranus > Neptune > Earth > Venus > Mars > Mercury > Pluto. - Broader Connection: - Links to solar system questions (e.g., Q12 [1997] on asteroids) or planetary classification, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to Pluto’s reclassification debate. - Key Takeaway: - Matching planetary characteristics (size, position) reflects 1998 understanding, with Pluto as smallest. - [1999] - Q23: Physical regions marked as 1, 2, 3, & 4 on the given map are respectively: - - Options: (a) Andes, Brazilian Shield, Guyana Highlands & Amazon Basin (b) Andes, Guyana Highlands, Brazilian Shield & Amazon Basin (c) Amazon Basin, Guyana Highlands, Brazilian Shield & Andes (d) Guyana Highlands, Brazilian Shield, Andes & Amazon Basin - Answer: (a) Andes, Brazilian Shield, Guyana Highlands & Amazon Basin - Q25: Which one of the following scholars suggested the earth's origin from gases & dust particles? - Options: (a) James Jeans (b) H. Alfven (c) F. Hoyle (d) O. Schmidt - Answer: (d) O. Schmidt - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Otto Schmidt’s accretion theory (1940s) posits Earth formed from a solar nebula of gas and dust, condensing into planetesimals and planets, refining the nebular hypothesis. - Why Not Others?: - (a) James Jeans: - Incorrect—Jeans’ tidal theory (1910s) suggested a star’s gravity pulled material from the Sun, not gas/dust accretion. - (b) H. Alfven: - Incorrect—Alfven focused on plasma cosmology, not planetary formation. - (c) F. Hoyle: - Incorrect—Hoyle worked on nucleosynthesis and steady-state cosmology, not dust-based origins. - Related Concepts: - Nebular Hypothesis: - Originated with Kant/Laplace, refined by Schmidt. - Planetesimals: - Small bodies forming planets. - Broader Connection: - Links to astronomy (e.g., Q22 [1998] on planets) or cosmogony, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to exoplanet formation models. - Key Takeaway: - Schmidt’s gas and dust accretion theory is the accepted model for Earth’s origin, distinct from tidal or cosmological theories. - Q26: In the given map, which one of the following pairs of ocean currents are shown? - - Options: (a) Benguela & Falkland (b) Canary & Humboldt (c) Agulhas & Guinea (d) Benguela & Guinea - Answer: (d) Benguela & Guinea - Q27: Which one of the areas marked as A, B, C & D in the given figure of the cyclone, witnesses heavy torrential short duration rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms? - - Options: (a) A (b) B (c) C (d) D - Answer: (b) B - Q28: Consider the following temperature & rainfall data: - Month | Temp. (°C) | Rainfall (cm) January | 6.7 | 14.0 February | 6.7 | 13.2 March | 7.2 | 11.4 April | 8.9 | 9.4 May | 11.1 | 8.1 June | 13.9 | 8.1 July | 15.0 | 9.6 August | 15.0 | 12.2 September | 13.9 | 10.4 October | 11.1 | 14.4 November | 8.9 | 14.0 December | 7.8 | 16.8 - The climate to which this data pertains is: - Options: (a) St. Lawrence type (b) China type (c) West European type (d) Mediterranean type - Answer: (c) West European type - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - West European type (Cfb, Köppen), in northwest Europe (e.g., UK, Ireland), has mild temperatures (6.7-15°C) and even rainfall (~141.6 cm annually) due to westerly winds and oceanic influence (North Atlantic Drift). - Data shows cool summers (15°C max) and mild winters, with consistent rainfall, matching West European type. - Why Not Others?: - (a) St. Lawrence type: - Incorrect—St. Lawrence (Dfb) has colder winters (below -3°C), less rainfall, typical of eastern Canada. - (b) China type: - Incorrect—China type (Cwa) has warmer summers (~27°C), summer rainfall peak (see Q21 [1998]). - (d) Mediterranean type: - Incorrect—Mediterranean (Csa/Csb) has dry summers, wet winters, unlike even rainfall here. - Related Concepts: - Oceanic Climate: - Driven by warm ocean currents. - Similar Regions: - Coastal Norway, New Zealand’s west coast. - Broader Connection: - Links to climatic zones (e.g., Q21 [1998] on China type) or ocean-atmosphere interactions, key for UPSC geography. - Relevant to temperate agriculture and urban planning. - Key Takeaway: - West European type climate, with mild temperatures and year-round rainfall, matches the data, distinct from colder, seasonal, or dry climates. - Q29: At which one of the following positions shown in the diagram will the height of the ocean tide be maximum? - - Options: (a) M1 (b) M2 (c) M3 (d) M4 - Answer: (d) M4 - Q30: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: - List-I (Timber): A. Cedar B. Douglas Fir C. Mahogany D. Teak - List-II (Country): 1. Myanmar 2. Canada 3. Mexico 4. Honduras - Options: (a) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4 (b) A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1 (c) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1 (d) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4 - Answer: (b) A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1 - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - Timber species and regions: - A. Cedar: Mexico (e.g., Cedrela odorata), key in Central America. - B. Douglas Fir: Canada (British Columbia), major construction wood. - C. Mahogany: Honduras, renowned for Swietenia macrophylla. - D. Teak: Myanmar, leading exporter of Tectona grandis. - Correct: A-3 (Mexico), B-2 (Canada), C-4 (Honduras), D-1 (Myanmar). - Why Not Others?: - (a) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4: - Incorrect—Myanmar not primary for mahogany; Honduras not teak. - (c) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1: - Incorrect—Canada not cedar hub; Mexico not Douglas fir. - (d) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4: - Incorrect—Myanmar not mahogany; Honduras not teak. - Related Concepts: - Tropical Hardwoods: - Mahogany, teak for furniture, from rainforests. - Softwoods: - Cedar, Douglas fir for construction, from temperate forests. - Broader Connection: - Links to resource geography (e.g., Q24 [1999] on coal) or deforestation, key for UPSC economic geography. - Relevant to sustainable forestry and CITES regulations. - Key Takeaway: - Matching timber to countries highlights their ecological/economic roles, with Mexico, Canada, Honduras, and Myanmar as key sources. - [2000] - Q32: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Tides are of great help in navigation and fishing 2. High tide enables big ships to enter or leave the harbour safely 3. Tide prevents siltation in the harbours 4. Kandla and Diamond Harbour are tidal ports - Which of these statements are correct? - Options: (a) 1 & 4 (b) 2, 3 & 4 (c) 1, 2 & 3 (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - Tides, driven by Moon/Sun gravity, impact coasts: - Statement 1: True—Tides aid navigation (ship timing) and fishing (fish concentration). - Statement 2: True—High tides raise water levels, allowing large ships in shallow harbors. - Statement 3: True—Tidal currents flush sediment, reducing siltation. - Statement 4: True—Kandla (Gujarat), Diamond Harbour (West Bengal) rely on tides. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 & 4: - Incorrect—Excludes true statements 2, 3. - (b) 2, 3 & 4: - Incorrect—Excludes true statement 1. - (c) 1, 2 & 3: - Incorrect—Excludes true statement 4. - Related Concepts: - Tidal Ports: - Mumbai, Kolkata also tidal-dependent. - Tidal Energy: - Used for power in some regions. - Broader Connection: - Links to coastal geography (e.g., Q51 [2002] on lagoons) or ports, key for UPSC economic geography. - Relevant to maritime trade and harbor management. - Key Takeaway: - Tides support navigation, fishing, harbor access, and silt prevention, with Kandla and Diamond Harbour as tidal ports. - Q33: Consider the following statements about the 'Roaring Forties': - Statements: 1. They blow uninterrupted in the northern and Southern Hemispheres 2. They blow with great strength and constancy 3. Their direction is generally from north-west to east in the Southern Hemisphere 4. Overcast skies, rain and raw weather are generally associated with them - Which of these statements are correct? - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 2, 3 & 4 (c) 1, 3 & 4 (d) 1, 2 & 4 - Answer: (b) 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Geographical Context: - Roaring Forties are strong westerly winds at 40-50°S in the Southern Hemisphere, driven by minimal landmasses and strong pressure gradients. - Statement 1: False—Primarily Southern Hemisphere; Northern Hemisphere has landmasses disrupting such winds. - Statement 2: True—High speed (50-100 km/h) and consistency due to Coriolis effect. - Statement 3: True—Northwest to east in Southern Hemisphere, per Earth’s rotation. - Statement 4: True—Overcast skies, rain, storms from cyclonic activity. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1, 2 & 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1 false. - (c) 1, 3 & 4: - Incorrect—Statement 1 false. - (d) 1, 2 & 4: - Incorrect—Statement 1 false. - Related Concepts: - Other Westerlies: - Furious Fifties (50-60°S), Screaming Sixties (60-70°S). - Oceanic Circulation: - Forties drive Antarctic Circumpolar Current. - Broader Connection: - Links to meteorology (e.g., Q4 [1995] on Willy Willy) or ocean currents, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to maritime navigation and climate. - Key Takeaway: - Roaring Forties are strong, rainy westerlies in the Southern Hemisphere, not uninterrupted in the north. - [2001] - Q34: Which one of the following weather conditions is indicated by a sudden fall in barometer reading? - Options: (a) Stormy (b) Calm weather (c) Cold and dry weather (d) Hot and sunny weather - Answer: (a) Stormy - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - A sudden fall in barometer reading indicates a rapid drop in atmospheric pressure, signaling an approaching low-pressure system, typically associated with stormy weather (e.g., cyclones, thunderstorms). - Low pressure draws in moist air, leading to clouds and precipitation. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Calm weather: - Incorrect—Calm weather corresponds to high or stable pressure. - (c) Cold and dry weather: - Incorrect—Cold, dry conditions are linked to high-pressure systems. - (d) Hot and sunny weather: - Incorrect—Hot, sunny conditions occur under high pressure. - Related Concepts: - Barometric Pressure: - Measured in millibars; rapid drops indicate cyclonic activity. - Weather Maps: - Isobars show pressure systems (see Q11 [1997]). - Broader Connection: - Links to meteorology (e.g., Q11 [1997] on isopleth maps) or cyclones (e.g., Q4 [1995]), key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to weather forecasting and disaster preparedness. - Key Takeaway: - A sudden barometer fall signals stormy weather due to low-pressure systems, distinct from calm or clear conditions. - Q35: Who amongst the following was the first to state that the earth was spherical? - Options: (a) Aristotle (b) Copernicus (c) Ptolemy (d) Strabo - Answer: (a) Aristotle - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Aristotle (384-322 BCE) was the first to argue Earth is spherical, based on observations: lunar eclipse shadows (circular), changing constellations with latitude, and ships disappearing bottom-first over the horizon. - His work in “On the Heavens” laid groundwork for later astronomers. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Copernicus: - Incorrect—Copernicus (1473-1543) proposed heliocentrism, not Earth’s shape. - (c) Ptolemy: - Incorrect—Ptolemy (100-170 CE) assumed a spherical Earth but followed Aristotle. - (d) Strabo: - Incorrect—Strabo (64 BCE-24 CE), a geographer, described Earth’s features, not its shape. - Related Concepts: - Greek Astronomy: - Pythagoras also suggested a spherical Earth; Aristotle provided evidence. - Later Developments: - Eratosthenes measured Earth’s circumference (~240 BCE). - Broader Connection: - Links to historical geography (e.g., Q25 [1999] on Earth’s origin) or astronomy, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to the history of science and navigation. - Key Takeaway: - Aristotle’s evidence-based claim of a spherical Earth was a foundational step in astronomy, predating later scholars. - Q36: If the stars are seen to rise perpendicular to the horizon by an observer, he is located on the: - Options: (a) Equator (b) Tropic of Cancer (c) South Pole (d) North Pole - Answer: (a) Equator - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - At the equator (0° latitude), the celestial sphere’s axis is parallel to the horizon, causing stars to rise vertically (perpendicular to the horizon) as Earth rotates. - At other latitudes, stars rise at an angle, except at the poles where they circle the zenith or nadir. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Tropic of Cancer: - Incorrect—At 23.5°N, stars rise at an angle, not perpendicular. - (c) South Pole: - Incorrect—At 90°S, stars circle horizontally, not rising. - (d) North Pole: - Incorrect—At 90°N, stars circle horizontally, not rising. - Related Concepts: - Celestial Navigation: - Equatorial position simplifies star tracking. - Latitude Effects: - Star paths vary with observer’s latitude. - Broader Connection: - Links to astronomy (e.g., Q14 [1997] on stars) or navigation, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to understanding Earth’s rotation and sky observation. - Key Takeaway: - Only at the equator do stars rise perpendicular to the horizon, due to the celestial axis alignment. - Q37: Consider the following statements made about sedimentary rocks: - Statements: 1. Sedimentary rocks are formed at earth's surface by the hydrological system 2. Formation of sedimentary rocks involves the weathering of preexisting rocks 3. Sedimentary rocks contain fossils 4. Sedimentary rocks typically occur in layers - Which of these statements are correct? - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 1 & 4 (c) 2, 3 & 4 (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Sedimentary rocks form at Earth’s surface via the hydrological system: - Statement 1: True—Formed by deposition and compaction of sediments through water, wind, or ice. - Statement 2: True—Weathering (physical/chemical) of pre-existing rocks produces sediments. - Statement 3: True—Often contain fossils, as organisms are preserved in sediments (e.g., limestone). - Statement 4: True—Form in layers (strata) due to sequential deposition (e.g., sandstone, shale). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 & 2: - Incorrect—Excludes true statements 3, 4. - (b) 1 & 4: - Incorrect—Excludes true statements 2, 3. - (c) 2, 3 & 4: - Incorrect—Excludes true statement 1. - Related Concepts: - Types: - Clastic (sandstone), chemical (limestone), organic (coal). - Geological Record: - Sedimentary rocks preserve Earth’s history. - Broader Connection: - Links to geology (e.g., Q39 [2001] on quartzite) or paleontology, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to fossil fuels and stratigraphy. - Key Takeaway: - Sedimentary rocks, formed by hydrological processes, weathering, fossil preservation, and layering, are key to Earth’s surface geology. - Q38: Volcanic eruptions do not occur in: - Options: (a) Baltic Sea (b) Black Sea (c) Caribbean Sea (d) Caspian Sea - Answer: (a) Baltic Sea - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Volcanic eruptions typically occur along tectonic plate boundaries or geological hotspots, often in geologically active oceanic regions. - Baltic Sea: Part of the East European Craton, one of the most geologically stable regions with no known volcanic activity. - Black Sea: Although relatively tectonically stable, it is located near the collision zone of the Eurasian and Anatolian plates, and has some deep-seated geological complexity, including potential ancient volcanism. - Caribbean Sea: Highly volcanic due to the subduction of the Atlantic plate beneath the Caribbean plate; includes active volcanoes like Soufrière Hills in Montserrat and La Soufrière in St. Vincent. - Caspian Sea: An inland basin on stable continental crust, but it lies near tectonic fault zones with some seismic activity. - Among these, the Baltic Sea is the most geologically stable and least associated with any form of volcanism. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Black Sea: - Incorrect—While relatively inactive, it is located near tectonic boundaries and may host some submarine volcanic features or ancient activity. - (c) Caribbean Sea: - Incorrect—A volcanically active zone with frequent eruptions and seismic events. - (d) Caspian Sea: - Incorrect—Though largely inactive volcanically, the region has some tectonic instability and seismic activity. - Related Concepts: - Plate Tectonics: - Subduction zones, mid-ocean ridges, and hotspots are primary locations for volcanic activity. - Stable Cratons: - Regions like the Baltic Shield are ancient, tectonically inactive zones with no volcanism. - Broader Connection: - Useful in physical geography, especially topics related to tectonics, volcanism, and geological hazards in UPSC. - Helps eliminate options in questions related to plate boundaries and geological formations. - Key Takeaway: - The Baltic Sea, being part of an ancient and tectonically stable craton, is not associated with any volcanic activity, unlike the other options. - Q39: Quartzite is metamorphosed from: - Options: (a) limestone (b) obsidian (c) sandstone (d) shale - Answer: (c) sandstone - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Quartzite is a metamorphic rock formed from sandstone (primarily quartz grains) under heat and pressure, recrystallizing into a hard, quartz-rich rock. - Sandstone’s high silica content transforms into quartzite’s interlocking quartz crystals. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Limestone: - Incorrect—Limestone (calcium carbonate) metamorphoses into marble. - (b) Obsidian: - Incorrect—Obsidian is volcanic glass (igneous), not metamorphic. - (c) Shale: - Incorrect—Shale metamorphoses into slate or schist. - Related Concepts: - Metamorphism: - Heat/pressure alters rock structure (e.g., regional/contact metamorphism). - Other Metamorphic Rocks: - Marble (limestone), gneiss (granite). - Broader Connection: - Links to geology (e.g., Q37 [2001] on sedimentary rocks) or rock cycle, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to construction materials and geological mapping. - Key Takeaway: - Quartzite forms from sandstone through metamorphism, distinct from limestone, obsidian, or shale transformations. - Q40: Identify the correct order of the process of soil-erosion from the following: - Options: (a) Splash erosion, Sheet erosion, Rill erosion, Gully erosion (b) Sheet erosion, Splash erosion, Gully erosion, Rill erosion - (c) Rill erosion, Gully erosion, Sheet erosion, Splash erosion - (d) Gully erosion, Rill erosion, Sheet erosion, Splash erosion - Answer: (a) Splash erosion, Sheet erosion, Rill erosion, Gully erosion - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Soil erosion progresses in stages: - Splash erosion: Raindrops dislodge soil particles. - Sheet erosion: Thin layers of soil removed uniformly. - Rill erosion: Small channels form from concentrated runoff. - Gully erosion: Large channels carved by intense water flow. - Sequence reflects increasing intensity and scale of water impact. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Sheet, Splash, Gully, Rill: - Incorrect—Splash precedes sheet; gully follows rill. - (c) Rill, Gully, Sheet, Splash: - Incorrect—Rill/gully are later stages; splash is first. - (d) Gully, Rill, Sheet, Splash: - Incorrect—Gully is last, not first; splash is initial. - Related Concepts: - Erosion Agents: - Water, wind, ice; water is primary here. - Soil Conservation: - Terracing, contour plowing prevent erosion. - Broader Connection: - Links to geomorphology (e.g., Q37 [2001] on rocks) or agriculture, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to land degradation and watershed management. - European patterns. - Q42: Assertion (A): During the neap tides, the high tide is lower and the low tide is higher than usual. - Reason (R): The neap tide, unlike the spring tide, occurs on the new moon instead of on the full moon. - Options: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A and R are true but R is NOT a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (c) A is true but R is false - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Tides result from gravitational forces of the Moon and Sun. Neap tides occur when Sun, Moon, and Earth form a right angle (first and third quarter moons), reducing tidal range: high tides are lower, low tides higher than average. - Assertion (A): True—Neap tides have a smaller tidal range, with moderated highs and lows. - Reason (R): False—Neap tides occur during quarter moons, not new moon. Spring tides occur on new and full moons, when Sun and Moon align. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R is false; it misstates neap tide timing. - (b) Both A and R are true but R is NOT a correct explanation of A: - Incorrect—R is false. - (d) A is false but R is true: - Incorrect—A is true; R is false. - Related Concepts: - Spring Tides: - Maximum tidal range during new/full moons. - Tidal Forces: - Gravitational pull varies with lunar phases. - Broader Connection: - Links to oceanography (e.g., Q32 [2000] on tides) or coastal geography, key for UPSC physical geography. - Relevant to navigation and tidal energy. - Key Takeaway: - Neap tides reduce tidal range but occur during quarter moons, not new moon, making A true and R false. - [2002] - Q43: Sun's halo is produced by the refraction of light in: - Options: (a) water vapour in Stratus clouds (b) ice crystals in Cirro-Cumulus clouds (c) ice crystals in Cirrus clouds (d) dust particles in Stratus clouds - Answer: (c) ice crystals in Cirrus clouds - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - A Sun’s halo is a 22° ring around the Sun caused by refraction of sunlight through hexagonal ice crystals in high-altitude Cirrus clouds (~5-10 km), acting as prisms. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Water vapour in Stratus clouds: - Incorrect—Stratus (low, 0-2 km) has water droplets, not ice; no refraction for halos. - (b) Ice crystals in Cirro-Cumulus clouds: - Incorrect—Cirro-Cumulus are high but puffy, with less consistent ice crystal alignment. - (d) Dust particles in Stratus clouds: - Incorrect—Dust scatters light; Stratus lacks ice for refraction. - Related Concepts: - Optical Phenomena: - Sundogs, coronas involve ice crystals. - Cloud Types: - Cirrus (icy, wispy), Stratus (low, layered). - Broader Connection: - Links to meteorology (e.g., Q34 [2001]) or atmospheric optics, key for UPSC geography. - Relevant to weather observation. - Key Takeaway: - Sun’s halo forms from ice crystal refraction in Cirrus clouds, not water vapour or dust. - Q44: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Ocean currents are slow-surface movement of water in the ocean 2. Ocean currents assist in maintaining the Earth's heat balance 3. Ocean currents are set in motion primarily by prevailing winds 4. Ocean currents are affected by the configuration of the ocean - Which of these statements are correct? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2, 3 and 4 (c) 1, 3 and 4 (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (b) 2, 3 and 4 - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Statement 1: False—Currents vary (e.g., Gulf Stream ~2 m/s is fast); include deep/surface currents. - Statement 2: True—Currents redistribute heat (e.g., Gulf Stream warms Europe). - Statement 3: True—Winds (trade winds, westerlies) drive surface currents. - Statement 4: True—Ocean basin shape, coastlines affect currents (e.g., gyres). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Statement 1 false. - (c) 1, 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Statement 1 false. - (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Statement 1 false. - Related Concepts: - Thermohaline Circulation: - Deep currents driven by density. - Gyres: - Circular currents shaped by winds/continents. - Broader Connection: - Links to oceanography (e.g., Q10 [1997]) or climate, key for UPSC geography. - Relevant to global warming. - Key Takeaway: - Ocean currents regulate heat, are wind-driven, and shaped by ocean configuration, but not always slow. - Q45: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Taiga 2. Tropical Evergreen 3. Tropical Deciduous 4. Tundra - The correct sequence in decreasing order of the Albedo values of these ecosystems is: - Options: (a) 1, 4, 3, 2 (b) 4, 1, 2, 3 (c) 4, 1, 3, 2 (d) 1, 4, 2, 3 - Answer: (c) 4, 1, 3, 2 (book says option b, but all other online sources are saying option c) - Analysis: - Scientific Context: - Albedo is the reflectivity of a surface (higher = more reflection). Ecosystems’ albedo depends on vegetation/cover: - Tundra (4): High (~0.6-0.8) due to snow/ice. - Taiga (1): Moderate (~0.2-0.4) with coniferous forests, snow in winter. - Tropical Deciduous (3): Lower (~0.15-0.2) due to seasonal leaf loss, less reflective. - Tropical Evergreen (2): Lowest (~0.1-0.15) with dense, dark canopy. - Sequence: Tundra > Taiga > Tropical Deciduous > Tropical Evergreen. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1, 4, 3, 2: - Incorrect—Tundra (4) has higher albedo than Taiga (1). - (b) 4, 1, 2, 3: - Incorrect—Tropical Evergreen (2) has lower albedo than Deciduous (3). - (d) 1, 4, 2, 3: - Incorrect—Tundra (4) has highest albedo, not Taiga (1). - Related Concepts: - Albedo Effect: - Influences climate (high albedo cools, low warms). - Biomes: - Ecosystems defined by climate/vegetation. - Broader Connection: - Links to ecology (e.g., Q8 [1996] on mangroves) or climate, key for UPSC geography. -
